It can be normal with Oakleaf Hydrangeas. My Snow Queen in Texas gets unusually warm and dry winters on some La Niña  years like this year (winter 2025-2026) and does the same thing. Some leaves turn 'on' their fall foliage as scheduled in the fall but many leaves remain shades of green too. Then a late freeze to the single digits arrives thanks to a polar vortex, we crash from the 60s/70s to the single digits overnight and the hydrangea finally goes to sleep in mid-late January or in February. Another Oakleaf, Pee Wee, located nearby but which gets less sun exposure, turns less of a fall leaf show but usually, many of its leaves stay attached and dark green. Toy Soldier and Ruby Slippers, in other locations, tended to drop the leaves after the fall foliage show was over instead. I do worry about the flower buds getting zapped as temperatures crash here from the 70s to single digits overnight but so far, they all bloom reliably in my zone 8. Snow Queen, et al will drop the old, still attached, leaves when it is time to open the leaf buds in mid March or so; that is when the Oakleafs usually break dormancy here. Big Leaf Hydrangeas can also remain with dark green leaves or basically, actively growing in the south until December and early-mid January here and in Florida so do not panic.

You are way ahead of yourself here, and only considering what is "pretty".  That's the least important choice here in a 40K install. The technical is more important, and limits the pretty. What is your humidity control like?  Even wide plank engineered will move around when there is too much swing in humidity.  The wider it is, the more you get gapping in low humidity and cupping in high humidity. Is your substrate gypcrete, as it is in so many condos?  That requires specialty installation, and wood is not the best option for that.  Does your community require sound abatement? Many do, which is why carpet is the default covering. The noise and echo of  hard surfaces doesn't' lend itself to multi family living.  Deadening the sound of hard surfaces requires a specialty install.  Are you a perfectionist when it comes to twice a day swiffering?  Clear, lightly grained wood, with no knots, shows EVERYTHING. The first little scrape you get will kill your soul, because it will be so much more visible against the calm grain look.  Grainier wood, like oak, tends to hide life, and wear and tear, a bit better. Rift and quartered oak can give you a calmer look that plain sawn oak, and disguise things better than a hard maple, or a much softer birch.

"The "solid, satisfying clack" if the old IBM keyboard is why I now use a mechanical keyboard" The clack is satisfying for sure, but it's the springs that make the old keyboards better -- better in this case meaning less physically taxing.  If someone isn't used to these, they initially may think their fingers/hands are working harder because it takes more downward force to push the keys, but because those springy springs push the fingers back up, it's actually less fatiguing on the hands if you do a lot of typing. Modern keyboards lack that strong spring mechanism of the old keyboards. I'll take my beat-up old IBMs any day over these "toys" they call keyboards nowadays or touchscreens. I have two old IBMs, one for both of my workstations. Used them all through my transcription years and they've travelled with me to every job I've had since, they've got to be 25-30 years old and still work perfectly. Since I've moved out of the big city (and I'm still 10 miles from my local small city with fewer options), I've become more desirous of more food/supplies in storage, rightly or wrongly. A standard fridge/freezer is fine, but I have an additional chest freezer to augment the bottom freezer of my standard unit.  I did that even when I lived in a big city, because I would often buy larger packages of meat and needed somewhere to store the extras - I also cook a lot and needed extra space to store frozen leftovers.   If I'm going to drive 40 minutes each way to the place that sells turkey wings, I'm going to buy at least a dozen at a time.   It's also often more economical to buy larger packages of meat, and I'm perfectly happy if my meat isn't cooked from fresh. There are some food items I use frequently but irregularly when I cook, so I always have at least a couple of these on hand:  chicken broth, canned tomatoes, and spaghetti sauce.   I don't plan meals ahead very often, so I don't know when I'll want them. I also like buying larger volumes of non-food items and storing them, more for the convenience of having to go out for them less often than because I fear running out.  I even get my toilet paper delivered to me 48 rolls at a time - it takes some storage, but I have to think about it less often.   So, big packages of garbage bags, paper towels, composting bags, dishwasher detergent, well water and furnace filters etc. I could store less, but that would mean I'd have to shop more frequently, and I just don't want to do that.   I may be in that position when I downsize to a small apartment (when the house is too much to care for), but for now I'll be more comfortable needing to shop less frequently.

Tartiflette.  It’s a heart attack in a casserole dish but once a year won’t kill you :-) Layer thinly sliced potatoes, carmelised onions and sliced Brie in a buttered shallow dish, seasoning as you go.  Pour milk or half and half to almost cover everything.  Top with grated cheese if you like.  Bake in a moderate oven until potatoes are soft. Cut a pocket into the side of a chicken breast. Stuff with sliced Brie and semi sundried tomatoes.  Tie firmly and saute in a shallow pan.  When nearly cooked through, add a hefty dollop of pesto to the pan and enough cream to make a sauce for the chicken.  Stir well until thickened. Pear, Brie and rocket/arugula salad with a light vinaigrette is nice.  If the rocket is too sharp for your taste, use half rocket and half baby spinach leaves. It’s a bit dated these days, but warm Brie with cranberry sauce on toast points is still pretty good –)

Let's see a photo....Wood does shrink and split from being too dry, it has for hundreds of years.  Controling humidity will stop that. You can put the Dutchman in from the bottom and not go all the way through, but a full through one is superior to  hold the joint.

Will there be seating at the island?  If so, then the island as drawn is not likely very functional storage-wise.  Full-depth base cabinets/drawer bases under the seating overhang (if there is one), will be very difficult to access.  Stick to no more than 15" deep cabinets or so. Regarding seating overhang - if you plan seating, the minimum recommended is 15" of clear leg/knee space.  If your family is tall or has long legs, more might be better.  Additionally, if there will be back-to-back seating at the island and a table in the Nook, aim for 60" b/w the table and the island overhang. If no seating is planned at the island, then back-to-back full-depth base cabs/drawer bases in the island will work.  In that case, the island's depth would be 4'3", not 4'6" (1.5" counter overhang in the front of the island + 24"D cabs/drawer bases + 24" cabs/drawer bases + 1.5" counter overhang on the back of the island = 51" = 4'3"). And, if no seating at the island, then 54" or so is all that will be needed b/w the table in the Nook and the counter overhang. Regarding the aisle b/w the island and a table in the Nook - since that appears to be the primary (and maybe only) access to the what I think is the backyard (top of the layout), that has the potential to be a busy aisle, so 54" if no island seating and 60" if island seating becomes important. Fruit flies are somewhat of a nuance once in a house and there are two ways I attack the invasion with 100% success  The first is simply using a vacuum cleaner and suck them up, they like to sit on cabinet edges and trim.  The other is a bucket with some kitchen vegetable and fruit scraps as bait.  I'll take it outside and spray the bucket inside and bait with permethrin, a safe and effective insecticide that will last weeks.  Then place it near the trash bin in the house and in a few days they're all gone.

IF they are fruit flies, they can be trapped by simply putting half a cup of water in a bowl or glass, add a squirt of dish washing soap and a couple of T of apple cider vinegar.  Leave it on the counter in the kitchen…..turn on a small light overnight.    If no flies are found on the bottom of the bowl in the morning……you don’t have fruit flies. Fungus gnats are another possibility, especially if you have houseplants.  They are likely to found in any room, near window sills. They look a lot like fruit flies to most. Another possibility, not as common, are drain flies which are likely to be found in a bathroom. You might investigate cluster flies, very common in some parts of the country.  They find attics in which to overwinter, coming out in roving gangs to annoy everybody. These guys look loke houseflies, but smaller.

The "Experts"  are generally insurance agents being paid on commission - Advantage plans generally offer a higher commission and are an easy sell with the low monthly premiums. " Initial Sales: Agents frequently earn significantly more, sometimes three times more, in the first year by selling a Medicare Advantage plan compared to a Medigap policy." Advantage plans are good for some people, especially those who are on a Medi Medi plan (Medicare/Medicaid) where Medicaid subsidizes the Medicare costs, but not the best for many others. Nerdwallet has a fairly good explanation of the differences. https://www.nerdwallet.com/insurance/medicare/learn/medicare-vs-medicare-advantage. I looked at the choices for my sister and a few friends in the past year and helped them evaluate their bottom line costs based on past and known medical issues. 1 was better off with a Medi-Medi plan.   The other 3 were all best served with a Plan N Medigap coverage.   (Plan N and Plan G are similar, and in the state where I live physicians are not allowed to charge "excess" charges that are covered under plan G and not covered by Plan N). You do need to understand the nuances of your particular circumstance to figure out what is best for you. When selecting the appropriate Part N plan I also looked at their historical rate increases year over year.   Some offered lower initial costs than the plan I recommended  (Mutual of Omaha), but the 5 year average was higher due to more rapidly increasing charges. Some agents also make recommendations based on biases that I am not sure they recognize.  One of the people I assisted met with an agent that had previously recommended a Medigap policy for another person I knew, but not only during the initial meeting, but again when we did a second meeting to finalize things he recommended a Medicare Advantage plan and mentioned the Silver Sneakers benefit.    The person was a black male who was a high school and college athlete.   His income wasn't as high as the previous person, but it was high enough that he would receive no extra benefits or reductions in costs based on income. 1st year the Advantage plan premium would have been $1200 less than the Part N, but he would have incurred $6000 in out of pocket costs as he needed knee replacement surgery.  It would take 5 years of reduced monthly payments to equal the savings he got the first year by purchasing the Plan N policy. I don't believe it was a conscious bias that made the agent offer the wrong plan, but subconsciously I think he equated black to being poor and equated someone in a blue collar job vs white collar job as poor, but we cannot make assumptions and need to actually evaluate plans based on income post retirement.     I called the agent privately after the 2nd meeting and expressed my concerns.   He was apologetic and I hope he learned from the experience.

Many people do not realize the change that has come to the Ohio area in the last 300 years.    At one time one of the major hindrances to travel in Northern Ohio was the great swamp,   This swamp extended on both sides of the Maumee River from about Fort Wayne to Toledo,  in places it was over 50 miles wide.    Starting about 1860 the swamp was gradually drained and today exist only in some preserves. If you are familiar with the Fort Wayne area.  the Swamp extended east from Fort Wayne in a V shape.  The edges being about US 30 on the south and Indiana 37 on the north.   With all of the farming in the last 100 years you can still see the ridges of earth that created the edge of the swamp.  Today what was the swamp is covered with many productive farms. There were smaller swamps along the edge of Lake Erie and along some of the other rivers in the state.

" Do we need to tell our aging children that they should be getting colonoscopies?  " Sometimes yes, sometimes no. An insight struck me when ours were entering teen years. I didn't have nagging parents who treated me like a kid, though my wife did and it was unpleasant for both of us. The insight I had was to treat child rearing and the instilling of the need for integrity, good values, good judgment and being sensible and thoughtful in their conduct as being akin to packing a lunch. When you pack a kid's lunch, you try to provide everything they later will  need and like but there's no guarantee they'll eat it. I figured that the "pencils down" point for the transferring of needed adult skills would be reached when they left the house for college, or otherwise. I wanted to do my best to provide everything they should need to live as happy and successful adults BEFORE they left home. After that, they would be making their own decisions. With little or no unwanted ongoing parenting. I was the philosophical/practical/life skills brainwashing parent between the two of us. I drove each of them in the morning to high school for several years, often a 25 minute trip, and that's when we had our talks. It did mostly seem to work, they're all reasonably happy and functioning adults who can manage their own affairs well and contribute to their communities.  An apparent recognition (and a pat on the back I gladly accept from time to time) is that while I rarely (never) offer unsolicited advice or comments to them, each periodically contacts me to present something they're thinking about or considering to ask for my view of it and any advice I would offer. What I see is vinyl siding, and the contractor put down a layer of 1/4" foam insulating (common),  followed by  Bildrite , a fiberboard used a lot from the 1950's into the early 80's, but lost favor to OSB board.  Wall studs are more than likely 2 x 4's based on the era suggested by the buidrite, and the insulation could be anywhere from zero to R11 (3 1/2"), followed by sheet rock.I've seen an entire subdivision built in the mid sixty with bildrite exterior sheathing with only 1" of fiberglass insulation in the walls, (not a typo, 1" thick insulation), so what you have can't be determined without cutting a hole in the sheet rock to see.If the insulation is little to none the best approach to fixing your problem is to remove the vinyl siding, tear off the bildrite and insulate from the outside, followed by sheathing the wall with OSB and residing.  You can also add up to a 1 1/2" foam insulation to the OSB followed by the vinyl siding.  (1" is the more common and someone should do this).If the wall insulation is sufficient, I'd still remove the siding and check the Buidrite to see if water has gotten wet and rotted out (common).  If OK, I'd sheath over the bildrite with OSB, then add at least 1" of foam insulation (taping the seams) followed by the vinyl siding.  I've done this to entire homes and much easier then adding insulation from the inside, with less of a mess compared to ripping out all the sheet rock from the inside.Corners are a big problem and often the leakiest and coldest part of the home's envelope pulling in cold air from numerous leaks, with a large thermal bridge area to the inside.   If you feel the wall corner a person can actually feel the effect as they move their hand across the wall and over the corner.  It's caused by how the corners are framed, and can be addressed when the walls are striped from the outside.  Stuffing insulation between the blocks of a three stick corner, and then caulking all cracks where the studs are nailed together will reduce air infiltration.  Once the wall is rebuilt and covered with foam insulation, with the seams taped, it will drastically reduce the thermal bridge to the inside, not only in the corners but over all the studs in the wall.

If cost is your issue, then by all means go from the inside.  When you're in the wall look to see how rotted the buldrite exterior fiberboard is so you can get a bid to replace it along with adding 1" of sheet foam when the house gets resided. Using sound building science may cost more but could be even more expensive if it isn't used.  When fiberglass insulation gets wet it loses it's insulation properties and causes permanent compaction that won't insulate, and also leading to a risk of mold growth.  You may find wet/compacted insulation for sure and maybe mold. The higher the humidity in a room the higher the vapor pressure will be forcing moisture into the walls, and in a laundry closet environment  it's going to be high, and it's going to be wet and compacted from being wet.  Hopefully you won't have any mold to deal with.  The only way you will avoid the same situation again is making sure the wall is completely sealed with a vapor barrier with seams taped all the way around,  even around the dryer vent through the wall.  For older homes It's a chore but can be done if the person doing it pays attention to details. At one time I tested the effects of adding just 1" of the EPS insulation board to the outside wall in the lower level of an unfinished split level compared to no exterior insulation.  The wall had no indoor vapor barrier and no sheet rock.  Over a very cold winter with some night time temperatures down to almost 20 below, the results were shocking. Behind the fiberglass insulation without the EPS insuation on the outside against the exterior sheathing the inside of the OSB board was very wet including the insulation with ice and very cold.  The area with the EPS insulation was only cool five inches into the fiberglass and completely dry.  Not even a sign of moisture condensing on the  OSB board.  The reason is the outside foam insulation effectively moving the dew point outside the structural wall  providing a thermal break and keeping the OSB warmer and dry. You only have a 3' section to do, and the walls can be sealed even better than going through the inside.  When considering removing all the sheet rock, pulling off the mill work, re sheet rocking, finishing, painting and putting the mill work back on (not even considering the loss of use and the mess), I don't believe going from the outside is any more expensive using less skilled workers on an entire home, you only have 3'. Opening the walls from the outside makes it easier and each cavity can be caulked at the stud with cut vapor barrier stuck to the caulk.  Rock wool or un-faced fiberglass is then stuck in the each cavity, a bead of caulk on the studs and the new OSB nailed on creates perfect dead air spaces, The new 1" foam insulation nailed on and taped and then the siding creates a superior envelope that never can be achieved by going through the inside.

Apricot trees are usually able to produce fruit without a pollinating partner, but the "Moongold" variety appears to be an exception to this. Probably almost any other apricot tree, provided it is a different variety, should be able to pollinate it. The issue will mainly be bloom time. Planning officers often reject flat-roof extensions on bungalows because the new eaves sit higher than the original and make the addition look disconnected from the house, so one compromise that usually works is keeping the modern look but visually lowering the extension by using a very shallow pitched or “mono-pitch” roof (almost flat but technically pitched), setting the roof below or close to the original eaves, and using one main material with subtle contrast for example rendered walls to match the bungalow with brick used as a feature band or courtyard wall rather than the whole extension. another common trick is stepping the extension down in sections or using setbacks from the front elevation, which reduces the “bulk” the planners mentioned while still giving a Scandinavian/organic modern style with large glazing, timber accents, and flat-looking rooflines if you want to keep a true flat roof, you might also propose a parapet edge that hides the roof height and aligns visually with the existing eaves, which sometimes satisfies planners because the extension no longer appears taller or “jarring” in the street scene.

I wouldn’t try and lift more of the herringbone, especially if it’s already that well bonded. You’ll likely do more damage than good. The neatest fix here is actually the simple one — bring the new floor forward and use a transition strip (threshold bar). It won’t look weird not being under a door. That’s quite common, especially where layouts have changed. What matters more is that the join looks intentional rather than patched. If you pick something that matches the wood tone (or even a slim metal trim if you prefer a modern look), it can actually look like a deliberate design break between two areas. Trying to perfectly join into that herringbone edge will be very difficult and rarely looks right unless it’s done from the start. The first thing I see is that the table is very large and creates an obstacle for entering the kitchen -- from every direction.  You have only 3' between the island and the table; imagine a person is sitting in a chair -- the aisle is completely blocked.  And it looks like less than 36" at the table corners.  You could shorten the cabinet run or go with an oval table, but you're not going to be happy with these bottlenecks. Second, you do not have space for seating at the island -- you do not have space in two directions:  At a 10' island, each of the six chairs you plan will have 20" of space.  The people in the middle won't be able to get in /out.  You could comfortably have four chairs in this width.  You need 5' of space behind island seating.  I'd fix this by cutting the island back to 36".  I can't comfortably reach across 45" anyway, and I don't want to walk around both sides when I'm cleaning.  36" will give you standard 24" cabinets on one side /12" of overhang for stools on the other side. While we're talking about 24" deep cabinets, be sure your drawers go all the way to the back of those cabinets.  I lived in my house for years before I realized I have 18" drawers in 24" deep cabinets.  Why?  I am no woodworker, but it seems they could be 22" deep -- and that extra space at the back would be welcome!  Also make sure you get full-extension drawers (so you don't have to fish around for things in the back-back of the drawers) and insist upon heavy-duty hardware, especially for larger drawers. Do you need island seating + a table RIGHT THERE?  I know you say you host large gatherings, but I know I would use the island for food /not seating.  I'd want both sides "open" so people could walk around and serve themselves. How would you lay out food for a crowd?  Where would you put your plates /silverware?  Would you add desserts to one end of the island, or would you want them in a different location?  What about drinks?  Think through exactly how you'd do this -- for everyday meals AND for big parties. This is a barrier island.  It divides the sink from the refrigerator, creating a need for extra steps.  It's just inconvenient. What I don't see /absolutely would not go without is a pantry.  You have a world of cabinets, which will cost a fortune -- I'd get a pantry in there somehow.  A pantry is BY FAR the best kitchen storage.  It's cheap to build, and it allows you to see allll your stuff at once.  It also allows you to close the door on a mess.  In a perfect pantry you'd have a small work counter, where you could leave a crockpot running or a pan of bread rising -- or, for a big party, you could leave desserts hidden away.  You could go with a wide reach-in pantry in the space behind the island seating -- OR you could shorten the room and place the pantry at the end, where you currently have the stove. No one needs a 60" range in a home ever . I ran a catering biz for 18 yrs with a 36" range and a double wall oven. You would be better off having a catered dinner for Christams once a year than the money on the range and the venting . And I've been baking wedding cakes for years in a 30" oven -- zero problems.  5-6 tiers -- it just takes planning.  Cooling space is a bigger problem. Yes, you could cater multiple big parties for less than this oversized kitchen will cost.  People say, "I want a big kitchen because I love to cook, and I have big groups!"  No -- you want an efficient kitchen with everything laid out "just right" so you don't have to take extra steps /so everything is right at your finger tips.  Loads of space is not a substitute for efficient planning. That bumpout is totally useless . Well, you can't place a small table in this area because it's the back door, but I do like that it allows plenty of space between the table and the door.  Regardless of whether you favor it, it exists -- removing it would cost more than keeping it, and it does add personality. We have entertained 7 times in the last month (more than normal). Usually its only 15-25 people, but can easily get over 40 when my wife's large family each bring their large families. Well, it's January -- we've just been through the holiday season, and you say this is more than normal for you.  I hear what you're saying, but what you're planning is a mess:  It's a bloated kitchen that' difficult to enter /lacks a pantry /has poor flow.  Keep at it -- this absolutely isn't "it".

I have candied citrus slices by first making a simple syrup (i use 1 part water: 1.5 parts sugar) cook med- lo heat to dissolve every sugar granule, raise heat and boil for a few minutes.  you can store this in the fridge. when I want to candy the citrus i put the syrup in a broad saute pan — you’ll need the syrup to be about 1/2” deep. slice citrus fairly thinly, cook at a bare simmer (so as not to damage the fruit) turning at least once. don’t crowd the pan with fruit.  i think you need to cook at least 15 minutes (maybe a bit longer) so the fruit looks well-permeated with syup.  dry on a rack overnight, the next day dredge in granulated sugar.  i store room temp between layers of parchment. the used syrup is handy for other purposes.

If you are already juggling plumbing, drywall and scheduling? A general contractor can save you a lot of coordination headaches. The biggest issue with bathroom projects is timing. One delay from a single trade can stall everything else. Here a simple way to decide: 1. If you want one person to manage all the trades?General contractor is the easiest route. They will handle the timeline, permits and make sure each trade shows up when needed. 2. If you are comfortable managing people yourselfHiring individual pros is fine. Many homeowners bring in: · A licensed plumber for the shower valve and tub · A tile specialist · A drywall finisher · A painter for moisture resistant bathroom paint and final touch ups This usually saves money but takes more time and planning. One thing people often overlook is the finishing stage. Bathrooms take a beating from humidity. So proper drywall repair and high quality interior paint make a big difference in preventing peeling and mildew. Here a helpful resource or services that explain the interior painting remodel in simple terms. Whether you go with a GC or separate trades, just make sure the final finish looks clean since that’s what you see every day.

When I was a teenager living in a much colder climate than the one I live in now, many gardeners bought into the whole "winterize your roses" concept (a concept I believe was manufactured by the companies that made the winterization technologies that were being promoted), myself included. Yeah, I'd buy those paper or plastic cones and collars and heap up soil 8" deep around the crown, cover with leaves, etc, etc. Many roses barely survived the winter anyway. (I remember both 'Tiffany' and 'Peace' survived 2 or 3 winters at most) But at some point I stopped doing it because it was tedious and I became involved in other things. Ya know what? It turns out it did not make one bit of difference if I did or didn't "winterize" the roses I had. The ones that were least suited to the climate died after 1, 2 or 3 years, and the ones that were appropriate for that climate did just fine without any fuss. I still have a piece of the original 'Hansa' my grandmother and I planted when I was about 14. Yah, don't ask how long ago that was! I would say that if someone has established roses that are ten to thirty years old that prosper in the climate they're grown in, then they are sufficiently hardy for that zone and winterizing those roses is probably completely unnecessary — it's more of a case of the gardener feeling that they are actively participating in the survival of those roses. But I seriously doubt that any rose that has lived thirty years where they are planted, requires any special handling to get them through the winter. But do whatever makes you feel that you're doing the right thing for your garden. No one else has the authority to dictate our garden techniques or our choices. Do what makes you happy.

There are going to be 40 different answers if you ask 40 different people. Paint Talk is a good forum where you can read the advice professional painters are giving each other.    They don't all agree.   Some don't prime new drywall at all, most do.   Most seem to shy away from the PVA primers and go for an all purpose primer.   Quite a few swear by Gardz.   Some  use Gardz and then paint a white primer over it since it is transparent and makes seeing flaws a bit difficult. When doing my own home I have not started with level 5 walls, so I can get away with a few things that you can't get away with if your are working with level 5 walls.   I still always wipe down my walls with a damp cloth to get rid of any dust before painting.    I don't sand between coats, but I would if I had level 5 walls. I always use one coat of primer and 2 coats of paint. I use Zinsser 123 for the walls that were not wallpapered.   I am using Gardz on the walls that were previously wall papered.   I am using BM Regal Select for my walls and Advance for my doors and trim.   I am not thrilled with Advance, and am looking at some alternatives. I have noticed some micro bubbles in Advance - most of which pop on their own within seconds of applying the paint, but I have to check the surface and use a insulin needle to pop those that have not popped so I don't see them in the finished work.  PITA On my exterior garage door and windows I used SW Duration. The one thing you will never see when I have completed a room is sloppy paint - no ceiling paint on the walls, a hairline of wall paint on the ceiling, lines between trim and walls are clean and straight. I think this is what I find most annoying when people hire pros to do their painting.  I know people who spent a fortune on the highest end paints and the finished work isn't perfectly clean.  Little drips, patches that weren't sanded well enough to appear smooth or were sanded and not textured to match the wall, outlets that have paint on them and my biggest pet peeve is ceiling paint that has gotten on the wall.   Why is it so hard to make sure the line goes on the ceiling where the eye doesn't see it? I get complements on my paint jobs from the trades people I know all the time. Each person has to know what is important to them and just how fussy they need to be to be happy with the end result. If you are hiring someone to paint I would demand that they do a primer and 2 coats of paint.  I would not specify which primer, but explain that you don't want to see any flashing where the drywall has been taped.     I also find that many painters use less product than they should.   Estimate the number of gallons needed and see how much they use.   If they spread the paint too thin it doesn't hold up as well or cover as well.   This is the main reason painters need to do a third coat of anything - if they used the appropriate amount of paint and primer 1 coat of primer and 2 coats of paint will cover.

Due to my systemic mastocytosis (a form of mast cell disease - SM is very rare and is responsible for many of my other health issues), I have never been able to use mascara/eye liner/eye shadow because they all cause eye irritation (I didn't know that was the cause until 2017- I just knew that my eyes would be irritated after use). Luckily, I have naturally long/dark eyelashes + people think that I'm wearing eyeliner even though I don't ever.  I also still have pretty nice eyebrows  - I never did the 90s over plucking (plus I'm half Italian - I think that helped with my eyelashes and eyebrows). However, I decided to try Latisse back in 2011 or so (who doesn't want even longer/fuller eyelashes???!!). After about three months, I noticed that my eyelids had a bit of a reddish brown tint.  I confirmed that it was a potential side effect of using Latisse - so, I stopped using it and my eyelids turned back to normal skin color after a few months. I have a Chem Engineering undergrad degree (originally, I wanted to go to med school - but then I wasn't sure - so, I switched from Human Biology to Chem E just in case I didn't go to med school - and then wound up attending law school instead).  So, I started doing some research related to Latisse (bimatoprost). I learned about side effects related to the use of bimatoprost for glaucoma.  Most of these side effects were not disclosed related to using Latisse. Bimatoprost belongs to a class of medications called prostaglandin analogs (PGAs).  The side effects of PGAs are significantly risky + they extend far beyond the minor side effects acknowledged in marketing materials. From "panda eyes" (darkening of upper and lower eyelids), itchy, red, dry eyes to permanent iris color changes to significant orbital fat atrophy.  This condition, often termed prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy (PAP), results in a sunken, hollowed, or aged appearance around the eyes. There is also potential thinning of eyelid skin + periocular muscle atrophy and weakness = upper eyelid ptosis (drooping). I know someone who had to have surgery to address the atrophy related to her right eye muscles. MANY products sold on Amazon (+ at other retailers) as lash/eyebrow growth serums also contain PGAs.  My sister was using one that is pretty popular (I can't remember the name).  I read the ingredients - and told her to stop using it - unless she wanted permanent changes (many of which not only age a person's appearance, but can have life altering effects). While using these type products on your eyebrow area could prevent some of the side effects - there is still PAP and periorbital muscle atrophy/weakness that has occurred + skin discoloration. Sorry for the long comment.  This is just a subject that is very upsetting to me.  I believe that I have dry eyes as a permanent side effect + I had to do a lot of eye muscle exercises in order to strengthen my right eye muscles (I still do them now - but on both eyes just to keep the muscles strong in order to prevent drooping eyelids).

A loud bathroom exhaust fan usually signals dirt buildup, loose parts (housing, motor, blades, ductwork), or worn-out bearings, often identified by rattling (loose parts/duct), grinding (blade rubbing/bad bearing), or humming (motor/electrical issue). To fix, first, shut off power, then clean dust from the grille, blades, and motor with a brush/vacuum; if noise continues, check and tighten mounting screws, secure loose ductwork (maybe add insulation), and try oiling motor bearings with light machine oil (like 3-in-1) before considering replacement, especially if the fan is old (10+ years) or ineffective

It's really amazing the misinformation that is promulgated by so called professionals, like the fabricator in a previous post.  Beth is correct--there's no such thing as "hard marble." Found this regarding flavor, FWIW. Flavor Showdown: How Do They Taste? When it comes to taste, Japanese Wagyu and American Wagyu are notably different. Japanese Wagyu delivers a luxurious, buttery flavor that’s more about the richness of fat than the punch of beef. The meat melts at lower temperatures due to its high concentration of monounsaturated fats — meaning every bite virtually dissolves on your tongue. If you want a steak that satisfies your carnivorous instincts with a luxurious twist, go American.

With a room that has multiple traffic paths, the best approach is to treat the furniture layout like a “floating island” seating zone instead of pushing everything to walls. Your fireplace/TV is still the focal point, but it doesn’t mean the furniture must be perfectly symmetrical to the whole room, it just needs to feel intentional within the seating zone. One strong solution is to center the rug + main seating group around the fireplace, and then use a sofa table/console behind the sofa (or behind a loveseat) to visually separate the family space from the kitchen path. That console also becomes functional “landing space” for lighting, drinks, or decor, and helps the seating zone feel anchored rather than drifting in a large open plan. Since your fireplace is off-center and you’re trying to keep the French door pathway usable, you don’t need to fight for perfect centering, instead, aim for clear circulation lanes (at least comfortable walking width) and define the conversation/TV zone with the rug and furniture angles. A few easy wins based on what commenters often spot in these rooms: reduce visual clutter, avoid awkward console placement behind smaller seating (if it blocks flow), and use a substantial lamp on the round side table to warm the space. Also, mounting the TV slightly lower and simplifying the mantle visual line can make the focal wall feel calmer, and once the focal wall is visually balanced, the whole room layout tends to “click” better.

Question 1: where would you put its humidistat? On the second floor where the supply and returns are? Or on the first floor, near the staircase, to sense the downstairs air? Question 2: HVAC installer is planning on tying the dehu condensate line to the heat pump condensate with a switch that shuts off both units in case of a leak. Is that the right way to do this? Or do they each need a separate condensate drain line and separate switches? First off any time I am going to recommend a dehumidifier I tell people that while a dehumidifier is the right approach to "control" humidity in the home this control is greatly dependant on sizing and how those controls are employed... also that using such a device will make your electrical bill go up depending largely on set points not to mention appropriate sizing. (For those reasons I am more likely to recommend an Inverter Heat Pump like the Bosch) while the Bosch Inverter won't control humidity like a dedicated dehumidifier will most of the time it's good enough and your electric bill goes down instead of up AND then you don't have yet another function of your HVAC system to replace / repair / maintain so often. (Bosch BOVA 2.0) This morning my office is 55% RH at 69F so a bit on the high side for humidity, but chilly running in heat mode currently. (usually during the summer my RH levels just running the Bosch only are almost always around 40-45% RH. Also warranties for these kinds of appliances is less than what some would think most of the time uusally 5 years. They rarely last much longer than 5 years... so you're never done paying for one of these. Question 1: Some units come with a set point control on the unit itself, although if it were me I would use a humidistat placed near the return (where your filters go) and near your thermostat that controls your HVAC system. Question 2: Heat pumps are only going to create condensate on the inside of the home during air conditioning mode, in heating mode all the condensation (usually in the form of ice if it's cold enough outside will form on the outdoor coil) otherwise it just drains off on the ground. Tying the humidifier drain to your heat pump's AC condensate drain / along with cut out protection in case the drain clogs would be appropriate in my opinion. Also the picture you show is wrong in my opinion, the unit should sit in a drain pan of some kind when being placed in an attic. I service the Katy, Texas area.

Thank you so much! I agree about the increased electric and that’s a concern. We’re running two, 2 ton Rheem inverter heat pumps so hopefully as you say they will do the majority of the work. Luba, in the realm of "inverter driven" whatever it be either heat pump or air conditioning is greatly dependant on the algorithm of the drive. So with this in mind a manufacturer can say "inverter driven" even if the unit in question has more than 2 speeds to differeniate it from an older less efficient 2 speed unit. (this is typically referring to speeds of the compressor as all the other motors are variable speed already. Rheem makes a slew of different inverter driven heat pumps and their upper product lines (most efficient) specify operation of between 40 and 110% with no specification as to how that operation is achieved. (If they don't say it, then it's probably not true) Which was why when I stated the Bosch, I also included the model # BOVA 2.0 (because Bosch makes cheaper models that don't perform as well over cost / separation from the upper model. (you get what you pay for kind of stuff) So what I have found is good news bad news as it plays out with the Rheem brand. The highend model RP19AY is limited. In their words: Variable Speed Scroll Compressor & Inverter Drive: — Features variable speed operation from 40 to 100% capacity with the EcoNet ® Smart Thermostat — Offers overdrive capability up to 115% to maintain performance in extreme conditions — Provides precise temperature control, advanced humidity control and greater efficiency What all that doesn't say is how does it do it?, which is important as this could merely be a 5 staged "inverter driven" machine. Which isn't like bad, but no where near Bosch BOVA 2.0 with start up at around 20-25% and then 1% steps up and down. "Inverter driven is expensive in terms of components and the the drive is what determines how good it truly is" How much worse could it be with the Rheem if you have an even lower end model that is "Inverter driven" RP16AZ Inverter driven The paragraph above is in the manufacturers words... what I know from years gone by is that Rheem, Ruud has mostly gone to inverter driven machines and the lower end of the model spectrum they offer is typically nothing more than a 3 speed machine. I suspect this RP16AZ is none other where the unit starts out at 45%, then switches to 70% and finally if the load is heavy enough ramps to 100% and that's it. Which essentially is "inverter 3 speed". In comparison to the Bosch? In a 2 ton? well the Bosch doesn't make a 2 ton, it's a 3 ton configured at install to run in 2 ton mode, from there upwards of 74 speeds, starting from about 20-25% at start up. In terms of dehumidification needs and the little "why can't my air conditioner" dehumidify? It's not that it can't it's just that due to how / how long it runs greatly influences how well or not so well it will dehumidify. (related to speeds of the compressor, less cooling (temp dropping) the more humidity gets removed. -- In air conditioning land, this isn't dehumidification control it is a by product of how the equipment runs. Because the faster the compressor runs in the case of an inverter driven machine, the less dehumidification will be performed as it will run into over cooling, rather than any real dehumidification. Today in my office I am sitting at 45% RH at 70F. So you can see the difference a few days make from where I was when I initially made my first post to this thread. There can be days where I run a bit elevated, this is normal when trying to achieve dehumidification from a "high end -- premium inverter driven AC / Heat pump" and it's just to tell you that just inverter driven terminology doesn't mean the same thing from one machine or even model of the machine in question. Carrier infinity is another famous example of 5 speed machine, inverter driven. Whether Carrier is still this way or not? I haven't looked in some time to see if they changed things up yet or not. (They came long before Bosch came to my market in 2019) Very few inverter models use 1% up and down stepping... which is the ultimate to live up to -- to have any real shot at better dehumidification without the added expense of a whole home dehumidifier. Hopefully this provides you with better understanding and so you'll realize any short comings your selected Model may have.

The whole point of soapstone is that it is impervious, impenetrable, unlike marble that is porous and prone to etching. You’re not sealing it. Oiling or waxing is something you do to achieve a look, not to protect the stone. Whether you choose oil (mineral oil), wax, or a combination of both, it’s all cosmetic. For more info on scratches, consult the video below.

10 year soapstone owner here.  Soapstone doesn’t need sealing.  It’s so dense that nothing can penetrate the surface.  It won’t stain or etch. As for “hardening“ soapstone, there’s no such thing.  There are varieties that are very soft and scratch and chip easily.  Others are quite hard, like Belvedere, Anastasia, and Stormy Black, which are quite difficult to scratch and chip.  Then, there are varieties that are somewhere in between.  To make sure you‘re purchasing a hard variety, the slab should’ve been tested for hardness with a scratch test. You can choose to oil your counters (I did at first), which will darken the stone and hasten the development of patina.  It takes a few weeks for the mineral oil to stop evaporating, so you’d have to keep at it daily.  However, oiling will not harden the stone.

Wonderful that you are open to multi-generational living. I cannot read your plan.  Can you post it as another kind of file?  And, can you outline in a color the area where you wish to build? Two years ago, we created a suite, including kitchenette for my parents in their 80s should they ever need to come live with us.  I did loads of research including hiring an occupational therapist design specialist, and consulted my Dad, who has worked as an engineer on over 100 buildings that are ADA compliant. Falls are the most significant factor in precipitating decline in the elderly.  You want minimize fall risk in every decision you make.  Having wide, easy walking pathways is very important.  And you will need additional width to all circulation pathways to accommodate walker usage should they need one. You want to reduce distance needed to walk to the bathroom.  Urgency and frequency become issues with age and you don't want to create a long walk to the bathroom that encourages hurrying and increases fall risk. Consider how well you can achieve these needs in an 11 foot width shotgun layout.  The words LONG and NARROW are immediate red flags.  Perhaps you can think more creatively about where they should dwell.  Maybe they live in the primary suite and you and your spouse live in this new addition?  Or some other such swapping of space. Think hard about this. Also... 1. Do not build a bathroom to ADA specs.  They are created to suit the common denominator -- the average person in the general public.  Instead, base your height and spacing on the actual needs and height of your in-laws. Do they have degenerative diseases that will likely result in wheelchair usage?  If not, then don't build for wheelchair.  Only 7% of seniors end up needing a wheel chair.  Instead install grab bars for THEIR arm reach height, place sinks at THEIR height needs.  Allow enough room in a bathroom for a caregiver to assist with toileting and shower, room to park walkers, etc. 2. Have doors open out instead of into a room.  Should they fall and block a doorway, you don't want them trapped inside. 3. Get apple watches for them that will alert you if they have fallen.  You can live in the same house and still not hear someone yelling in the night because they have fallen. 4. Excellent daytime and nighttime lighting is key to reducing falls. There are loads of other tips to making a senior friendly living space but they are cart before the horse at this stage of your planning.

Yes!  I live in a blackspot prone area (Seattle) and spraying my roses with lime sulfur spray has made ALL THE DIFFERENCE in the health of my roses. Usually, it is recommended to spray roses three times: at the end of the season, in winter, and right after pruning in late winter early spring.  You spray the canes AND the soil around the canes (blackpost migrates from the soil up to the leaves).  As a bonus, the spray also smothers eggs from pests. Lime sulfur is actually not sold in Washington state unless you have a special agricultural license.  The reasons is, it contains lye, which has been deemed too dangerous for us Washingtonians to handle :))  I buy mine online and have it shipped to my house...no problem. It's probably easy to get everywhere else. I would rate dormant spraying as a GAMECHANGER in my rose growing journey. Your Rosanna is beautiful!

The main thing I have learned after inheriting a garden with lots of roses in it already which were planted in the prior 80 ish years, and then gardening for 35 years, is that there is NO one way to prune roses. It depends entirely on WHAT KIND of rose it is, and your climate. I always cringe in the very early Spring here (Northern  Calif, zone 9/10, Mediterranean climate) when the local Rose society, and some nurseries, put on free classes on "how to prune roses". These usually are really  classes on "How to prune modern hybrid tea roses". They do a fine job on that, but that ignores the several other classes of roses which actually prefer our type of climate over any other, and thrive here with much less fussing. The old tea roses and old hybrid china roses which thrive in my garden do NOT want to be pruned hard like modern hybrid teas. Over the years when one of those inadvertantly DID get hard pruned, they sulked for actual years before gradually recovering, if they did indeed recover.  The ones in my garden like to be mainly left alone, other than taking out dead wood (sometimes this is not even a good idea, if a large bush has built up dead wood as a sort of scafolding support under the rest of the bush), shaping a bit, and keeping them OFF of the driveway and paths (some of the old teas and chinas have "I am going to conquer the world"complexes). The old Vintage Roses catalog has wonderful drawings of each type of old rose, its growth habit, and how to prune it if you want to. I do have a very few HTs, all surviors from previous generations of my DH's family. Interestingly, most of the bush types of those have died. The ones still alive are all climbers. I think that most of those started out as bushes, and then reverted to climbing because of local conditions. Of course, then do need pruning, tying up, etc. We have lots of other types of old roses, and none of them react well by being pruned according to the "rules" for pruning HTs bushes. It depends on their growth habit mainly. Some old polyanthas I have grown like Cl Cecile Brunner have tried to eat our three story house . Others like Schmidt's Smooth Yellow stay a nice neat 4' tall. I only learned how to treat all of the various old roses in my garden by "trial and error", mostly error in the begining until I started paying more attention. Jackie

The rose is losing more moisture through the canes than it is able to absorb through the roots. IF the bare root contains sufficient resources upon receipt AND the weather conditions are sufficiently cool and damp, they can be planted with the canes exposed to the air and survive. If it doesn't, or if the conditions under which it is attempted to be grown are too warm/hot, sunny and dry, it will utilize the resources it contains to struggle to survive, often at the expense of putting out new roots to enable it to support itself. I have, for more than forty years, planted bare roots by mounding them with either mulch or potting soil, only leaving the top inch to two inches of the canes exposed to the air/sun. Keeping the plant cool, damp and dark will stimulate it to produce roots. Exposing the canes to sun and warmth stimulates it to produce leaves and canes. If it either contains insufficient moisture and/or food to do it, or hasn't sufficient feeder roots with which to absorb what it needs, it simply dries out and either turns brown or black, until it dries out and dies.  Leaving the top inch or two exposed to the sunlight and warmth will allow the plant to grow roots until it has enough sap pressure from water being absorbed by the new feeder roots to push new growth from the exposed cane tips. As that new growth begins, you gradually expose them to the hotter, brighter, drier air a very few inches at a time, every few days until the plant is fully exposed to them so it hardens off slowly, preventing it from being burned by the hotter sun and drier air. You can accomplish this in that pot by obtaining some corrugated card board, say from card board boxes or using multiple sheets of news paper or even roofing paper and create a cylinder of the material large enough to fit around the circumference of the plant and tall enough to be inserted into the soil ball inside the pot and only leave the two perhaps two inches of the canes protruding from its top. Ideally, it will be the circumference of the inside of the pot so when you remove a few inches of the soil in the pot and insert the cylinder, the pot will help keep it closed (staple the top of the sides together to keep it a cylinder or tie strings around it to keep it closed). Replace the soil in the pot to begin filling the cylinder so you encapsulate the plant in damp, cool soil. You want the cylinder filled to nearly the top so only the very tops of the canes are exposed. Water the soil in the cylinder and keep filling as the soil settles until the plant is covered by damp soil, all but the top two inches of the canes. Keep it watered as you normally would and watch for new growth to begin appearing from the tops of any remaining GREEN canes. You can also accomplish this by literally burying the whole plant in the ground on its side for two or so weeks to rehydrate it, then planting it, either in the ground, mounding it with soil as described above. Take a look at this article. I "borrowed" this image from it, and am giving the article full credit for it.  http://www.easyrosegardening.com/planting-bare-root-roses.html#gallery[pageGallery]/1/ I haven't lost a bare root since I started mounding them at planting. That used to be actually instructed on body bag bare root rose and may still be. I haven't purchased one in years. If you mound the rose you've pictured and catch it before it reaches the point of no return, you can probably save it. If you don't mound it to rehydrate it and encourage it to produce roots, it's pretty much doomed.  If you plant them exposed in rainy weather, mounding isn't required as being bathed by rain will keep the plant sufficiently hydrated as it produces roots. Planting bare root roses and not mounding them is the #1 cause of dead bare roots in my experience. Having sold canned and bare root roses for years, I've seen MANY returned looking just like the one pictured in the original post and every one of them have been due to drying out before they could produce roots. Mounding it to prevent drying out until roots are formed will prevent loss. Good luck.

Does Massachusetts Need to Worry About the Lone Star Tick? 🔹 https://fun107.com/lone-star-tick-massachusetts/ Thomas Mather is a professor of plant sciences and entomology at the University of Rhode Island. He is the director of the university’s Center for Vector-Borne Disease and its TickEncounter Resource Center, and he says reports of the lone star tick have increased by 300% between 1999 and 2023. The name "lone star" comes from the distinctive white mark on the backs of female lone star ticks, and they are very aggressive once they find a host. “They can be in swarms,” Mather said. “When they get on you, they move very fast. When they latch onto your clothing, they can be underneath your shirt before you have a chance to see them.” The bite of a lone star tick causes alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) which is an allergy to alpha-gal, a sugar found in the tissues of all mammals except humans and other primates. “This can trigger an individual’s immune system to respond by producing antibodies against alpha-gal, a reaction called sensitization, since the immune system is now sensitive to alpha-gal,” according to EcoRI. In other words, the person who gets bit could become allergic to red meat, dairy, gelatin or other mammal-derived products. Are Lone Star Ticks in Massachusetts? Mather found that lone star ticks prefer to feed on white-tailed deer and use them as reproductive hosts. In a recent survey, lone star ticks were found in nearly 30 Rhode Island zip codes and they continue to move northeast due to the reproductive success of white-tailed deer. Massachusetts has no shortage of white-tailed deer, which means it is becoming likelier for humans to come in contact with lone star ticks. According to EcoRI, Mather is working closely with the CDC, the University of Massachusetts and Martha’s Vineyard to develop an action plan for AGS. “Once someone uses a tool like TickSpotters (and) sends us a picture of a lone star tick, we can get them a serum within 72 hours before they develop an antibody,” Mather said. It has to do with the feeding of grain and it's the same reason why farmed fish are not healthy and why so many people take Omega 3 in capsule form, though it's not at all clear that taking capsules can make up for a massively heavy omega 6 intake. Just to add, the paleo diet of mainly meat is absolutely nothing like what our early ancestors ate. (I speak here as someone with a MA from Harvard in Anthropology, specialty archaeology.)  Hunter and gathering people gorged on meat--when they had it.  But most of the diet was of vegetable origin and very high in fiber.  Arctic peoples, of course, ate an entirely meat diet--but they and their lifestyle was highly specialized for their very extreme climate and the demands it made on their bodies.

I live in a small town.   The highest producing agent is the one who is contracted to sell new homes through the largest builder in our area.   Over 1/2 of her listings are the new builds, then she often gets the listing for the buyers house who is looking to buy one of her new build houses. Brokers are often counted as part of the transaction for each of the realtors working under them.   So the broker with 10 agents gets credited with all of their listings, while the individual agents get credited only with the sales they personally worked. Other top producing agents are often working as part of a team.  They may have an assistant or multiple assistants doing the research and showing properties to buyers or doing the paperwork.   Not a bad thing, but I don't know that it increases the likelihood that your home will sell faster or slower or get a better price than the person who sells fewer homes. They offered cafeteria style help.  Need help with a form - pay a fee.  Need help pricing the house based on market comparisons - pay a fee. . . I honestly think this will replace listing realtors in the future.   My sister is currently looking to buy another home. Root pruning trees is method used on field grown trees that are to be balled and burlapped. A denser root ball allows the tree to spend more time at the nursery with a higher percentage rate of survival. A tree that is to be dug and immediately transplanted, if done in the spring when the tree is dormant, will sprout new roots from the cut ends and grow continuously during the following season So, imo, why cut the roots over and over for several years, when you can cut them once, move the tree and by Fall you'll have a semi established tree that will continue to elongate the new roots, that you grew all summer?

Just looking quickly at the design a couple of things immediately concern me, you have a gas hob, minimum distance to the extractor is 750mm [unless manufacturers instructions say otherwise], ie about 1650 from floor, standard gap between worktop to wall units is about 500mm ie 1400 from floor. position of ovens, no worktop near them, just not very functional. Quick google search on nolte and nobilia [kutchenhause], they're both mid range in the german market with Nolte being slightly higher spec, but they're high volume run of the mill kitchen companies. Personally, i've looked at various german kitchen brands at KBB trade shows and i just don't get it, they have some nice fronts. But the actual cabinets aren't that great [16mm board/hardboard backs and lack of interior colours] and on a par with your high street sheds. They do tend to work on a different door size [bigger] and shorter plinth/legs so they have a bigger cabinet height wise than uk kitchens, more choice of cabinet heights for base and wall units but an independant kitchen studio could make something very similar with a bit of imagination and i think you'd get a better quality kitchen.

I think the Germans don’t care about thickness of cabinets like the British manufacturers.   Instead they concentrate on strength- the board is a higher quality than used on thicker UK carcasses.  And in contrast to UK manufacturers they often rate the drawers and pullouts for different weights.  Pull outs in my kitchen are rated to 70KG and I’m unaware of any UK manufacturer building to this standard. It is true that UK manufacturers offer different carcase interior colours but the criticism that German manufacturers are the same quality as a high volume shed in the UK is untrue as they demonstrably have higher quality fronts, more choice of colours finishes, heights, interior options and better fixings. Personally I agree that the vertical embossed lines have greatest impact on the tall cabinets.   You should consider if you this part of the kitchen is darker and it has less impact.   You might consider swapping the cream for a richer or stronger colour because the high contrast is falling from fashion, and you may want to consider if the stools have more room at the other end of the island.You might also consider if the waterfall legs is properly seen- if not it maybe unnecessary expense.

Blum, Hettich, Grass all have concealed runners at 70kg as well as 40kg and 50kg and at variable legths up to 650mm all available as standard for independant kitchen suppliers. All the ironmongery thats in a german kitchen is available in the UK. Nobilia is the largest producer of kitchens in europe, google their figures and they're producing over 3500 kitchens per day/159000 cabinets per week. For the cabinet itself, German kitchens often use a higher density board and the structural strength comes from precision manufacturing factory assembled glue and dowelled cabinets and the back panel is not used for structural support making for a lighter cabinet. A UK cabinet [from an independant not a shed] does use the back panel as part of the structure and is also glue and dowelled, so i'd consider its a more rigid structure. Certainly a lot of the frontals available from German/Italian kitchens are better than UK kitchens but that depends on the style, if you look at a more traditional, shaker or in-frame kitchen i think you have more choice in UK suppliers. If you look at flat slab premium contemporary/true handleless styles then the frontals that German kitchens offer more choice and style, but a UK kitchen supplier with a bit of imagination can offer the same/similar if they search out the right suppliers/manufacturers. For the cabinet sizes, heights and widths are dictated by the door sizes available, cabinet depths are dictated by the worktop. German kitchens do have more variable heights, shorter plinth heights to maximise base unit storage for the same overall height, more choice of cabinet heights so they can focus on different heights of worktops in their kitchen design, they can even measure the customers height to work out the optimal height of the worktop for you. But again, if your kitchen designer has made to measure doors available these cabinet dimensions can be replicated, we just seem to be stuck in a traditional 150 plinth, 720 base cabinets, 575, 720 and 900 wall units and towers to suit, 560/570 deep base and 300 deep wall units mindset in the UK.

Some assumptions are being made with my response. The water leaking and ice damming are sort of related, but need to be understood separately. Water Leak: Your manufacturer's asphalt shingles are more than likely able to be installed on a 2:12 slope (the minimum). However, the underlayment requires specific installation in overlap or multiple layers, or using an ice and watershield under the entirety. That may not have been done. Ice Damming: That process can cause water to back up under asphalt shingles regardless of roof slope. But even if you repair the shingle underlayment properly for 2:12, you still don't want ice damming as water finds a way. And, fixing the cause has other benefits. Here it appears the cause is because you have an enclosed rafter assembly on a low ceiling. You would not have enough room for venting and/or enough R value of insulation, where in a snowy climate probably requires R60. So the conditioned room (warm) meets the roof sheathing (cold), causes enough melt, refreezes, cycles over again, and eventually backs up under shingles. Redo the roof pitch: That is a choice. Besides topping off the roof, it would require new walls to match the original house's top plate height (but would allow normal height windows and ceiling). But I would question if the foundation was done correctly, this type of addition is reminiscent of a DIY buildout of a former concrete slab patio.

This is purely conceptual — it’s not to scale (it’s based on the existing items shown in the drawing) and doesn’t take into account all property constraints or your specific priorities. This option would allow for greater flexibility in the bedroom layout (for example, centring the bed and accommodating larger storage units), while also making better use of the bathroom space. text: I garden in an entirely different growing zone than you do, but some of the same problems are universal for all rose growers regardless of location. If you have black spot, powdery mildew, and rust issues, so do I.  If not, you are very fortunate.  Almost any rose will work for you and be relatively disease free if your climate also has low humidity. As far as insect and spider mite issues, regardless of zone, they affect us all. We deal with them on an as needed basis.  I mostly use conventional means, after finding organic means unsatisfactory. Apricot Candy is one of my favorites.  It has to be for me to have four AC bushes in my modestly sized (55± rose bushes), garden.  In full open bloom, the ACs are breathtaking to me. One thing though is Apricot Candy's foliage, although the bush is vigorous and the foliage is abundant, it does not have a thick, leather-like texture.  During the heat of summertime, with daily high temps above 90°F (32.22°C), day after day, the lowest leaves, about 1/3 the way up a cane, will drop no matter how generously and regularly watered.  This leaf drop issue does not seem to inhibit rebloom on my ACs one bit, but their, 'naked lower legs,' are visually conspicuous by their leaves' absence.  Their dropping is not due to the consequences of black spot damage, because I spray a conventional fungicide diligently (🙄), all black spot season long.  It's the persistent, intense heat that is the culprit. Another thing about my beloved Apricot Candys is that their foliage is unfortunately black spot prone in my hot/humid summertime climate, but only  very moderately so.  I do spray every 10-14 days with a systemic containing a fungicide like tebuconazole, alternating formulas from different manufacturers to prevent fungicide resistance. Enjoy your Apricot Candy.  Hope it becomes one of your favorites! Moses.

Some have scent on the moss while others don't. It seems when Wichurana genes get into the mix, they "polish" all the plant parts and reduce or eliminate the moss. Mr. Moore raised Rugosa X Moss seedlings. Their moss smelled BAD. They stank. A number of more modern roses (not mosses) have scent glands on their sepals, ovaries and peduncles but not nearly as many as OGRs. The scent varies in strength and type depending upon the genes of the rose in question. @Paul Barden raised Lemon Moss, a modern moss mini https://www.helpmefind.com/gardening/l.php?l=2.59974.1&tab=1 whose moss possessed lemon and pine scents. I noticed in my exploration of R. Fedtschenkoana that some seedlings were very smooth and few were "mossy". DLFED 3 https://www.helpmefind.com/rose/l.php?l=2.63190&tab=1 had mossy buds. The "moss scent" of Fedtschenkoana is "Noble Fir with hardwood smoke". DLFED 3 is still "evergreen" but without the smoke element and further crosses with it and moderns which produced mossy buds altered the scent through various evergreen types (spruce, pine, etc.). Mr. Moore's Scarlet Moss had multiple doses of Dortmund in it with little scent. https://www.helpmefind.com/rose/l.php?l=2.5640 Paul's old web site, Old Garden Roses and Beyond, is archived on the Wayback Machine (Internet Archive). Here is a link to Mr. Moore's writings there. https://web.archive.org/web/20161208182907/http://paulbardenroses.com/ralphmoore/contents/index.html Scroll to the bottom of that page to the link to the rest of the site. On that page, scroll down to the "Resources Guide" drop down menu to find the Site Index which will take you anywhere you want to go on the site. You will find sections on mosses and all other types. You can find a number of mossed minis, also, in the miniature section. Scour this and you'll have a wealth of information you can explore to direct your moss interests.

Some of Ralph's primary Moss hybrids were monsters in Visalia, but not here. 12-59-10 struggles to maintain more than 3 or 4 canes and they tend to stay under 5 feet. "OM" was even worse — it died outside in the open garden and only survived in a large pot in a hoop house under plastic. Even now, it has only a few canes about 6 feet long. I've rarely gotten anything of value from "OM", and I don't think I have a single seedling from 12-59-10 that I kept, but if you worked really hard and grew hundreds of seedlings, you'd eventually find one or two keepers. There are better roses to work with. I found 'Dresden Doll' reliably bred mossed offspring, as did 'Condoleezza', but I no longer have 'Condoleezza' and I fear it is extinct. 'Scarlet Moss' has immense potential for breeding remontant modern Mosses. Circas 2010 I crossed it with Svejda's "L-83" and got several heavily mossed seedlings with a variety of peachy and crimson colors. I registered one of these two years ago: 'Carol Whitten'.  I would recommend 'Scarlet Moss' as worthy of serious consideration in a breeding program. I do still have 'Capitaine John Ingram' and it's very pretty, but I have never attempted to work with it. I have not seen it make seeds and I am uncertain about it's ability to generate viable pollen. @Ian Stewart: Zone 6 Western Kentucky, USA if it's a modern HT style mossed bloom you're looking to create, if you go back to 'Capitaine John Ingram', then you are really just reinventing the proverbial wheel. If I were wanting to start a new line with good color and mossing, I would mate 'Scarlet Moss' with something like 'Midnight Blue' and see what you get.

Pay for a thorough inspection.  While the required inspections in the US are pretty good, in England, a basic inspection was very limited.  We put an offer in on a house in England, got a thorough inspection and backed out, getting our deposit back.  Best money I've ever spent.  Look at the permits for renovation for your new house and the neighboring houses.  That might give you a few hints.  Septic is a big expense, so if you're not on city sewage, find out the age of the septic tank. You could have a house full of asbestos and lead paint.  Or those could be limited or absent. None of us know.  Your new neighbors might know, if all the houses were built by the same firm. The US has some pretty good disclosure laws, but those are much weaker in the UK.  So, it's hard for us to guide you to pitfalls, because we don't know the rules in Australia.  Would a seller have to disclose asbestos? But, everywhere in the world, a good and thorough inspection is worth the price.  We had someone send a camera up the chimeys and got the cost of fixing them off the price of the house we actually did buy (in the US).

It is just the current trend of "modern farmhouse," painted white (or black, of all things chosen as popular), which was taken originally to emulate a barn and has just gotten out of hand. I would also like to comment on the floor plans. I think they are done very well, and certainly by professionals. I would gladly rent with my family as a BNB, it works well for that. A couple comments though:

I think I'd go for version 3. It's worth noting that channeling rain away from the roof valley in V1, 2, and 4 will be a challenge. In a downpour, there will be a lot of water in that valley and if it overwhelms your gutters, you'll have a waterfall on those stairs.  That's why I like the version with one roof, not two.  If you're planning to rent the upstairs unit separately, so there are no internal stairs, that's going to be a serious problem. IMO, "timeless" is not a mix of 3 sidings, as found in V1, where you have horizontal, vertical and shingles in the gables.  That's trendy.  You have plenty of detail with the balconies that you don't need to gussy up your house with fussy windows, more than one type of siding or the trim in the gables.  Simple is classic and timeless, when married to a nicely proportioned house. I would simplify the windows.  Those prairie style windows don't belong on a beachside house and they are fussy, rather than elegant.  Just have plain glass.  If they are double-hung, that's fine.  Again, classic and timeless is simplicity and good design.  Your windows are nicely proportioned, spaced and sized.  You will, presumably have trim around them.  That's enough.

Gardengal, this dovetails with something I almost put in my original comment!   Let's divide mail order nurseries into two categories: ones I order from regularly, and semi-regularly.  An example of the regular category would be Camellia Forest...probably the only one in that category anymore.  (And this spring I won't be ordering from them, it will be my smallest spring order season in years for a variety of reasons)  For an example in the latter category: it's been a while since I ordered from, for example, Far Reaches.  Maybe two springs, so, spring 2024.  But I still visit their website quite often when I'm looking up a certain plant and it comes up in a google search.  This happened recently as I formulated my first Jelitto seeds order in several years.*  I'll browse around to see what they are offering an kick the tires, so to speak.  And guess what?  For almost every mail order website I've visited in the past year or so, including the two I named, I see more  'sold out' notifications than ever! Two ideas:  people like you are having more trouble finding interesting plants in local nurseries, so are having to turn to mail order retailers.  OR...it's a marketing thing...nurseries are just realizing if they leave up 'sold out' webpages it creates a cachet that makes it seem like 'time is running out' and fuels impulse buying.  For me it's created the impression that the COVID gardening boom hasn't died down as some might have expected it to.  I sure hope that's true.  HOWEVER, if that was the case, I feel like nurseries like Appeldoorn and Quackin Grass would be finding buyers, not closing outright.  Just as we assume most parents want their children to outlive them (!), I'm going to broadly assume most nurseries owners would like their nurseries to outlive them.  For those of us old enough to remember, that used to happen quite often. (nurseries being sold to other parties)  But now you're telling us that in one of the gardening hotbeds of the country, the PNW, it's harder to find rare and quality plants at local nurseries.  Hhhhmmmmm....so there are mixed messages out there, to be sure! I placed an order with Rhododendron Species Foundation this spring, and it just occurs to me that, as a registered non-profit, they might be the only mail order nursery whose [financial] books are open.  It _sure_ would be interesting to see their plant sales over the past 10 years and how they've grown (I would be almost certain**).  But I'm not going to bother going to their website and trying to find those financial disclosures.  If anyone else does, please report back! * I will footnote my own post here to say that, one reason I will be ordering less from certain PNW perennials retailers is I've pretty much 'explored' the 'corpus' of plants available from them; there's hardly a major category I'm interested in now that I haven't at least tried.  And what I'm finding with unnamed 'wild' varieties of perennials, is that it is better to plant scads of seedlings from Jelitto or whoever, with the hopes that genetic variation will bestow upon you, a form or two that likes your garden.  The PNW retailers, whether they like it or not, have no choice but to be selecting cultigens that grow well in their radically different summers. ** even 15 years ago, grumpy old Harold Greer, the one time I met him, complained to me about the economics of having to 'compete' with a non-profit mail order nursery.
