Hi! I’m an interior designer and I often get people coming to me for second opinions on floorplans — usually with exactly the feeling you’re describing, where something just doesn’t quite sit right. At first glance, Option A does have more positives than B, although there’s quite limited free worktop space around the cooker, which is always really useful to have. Overall, though, both options feel quite overcrowded. When spaces are pushed this hard, they can become difficult to use day to day and uncomfortable to move around in, even if everything technically “fits” on plan. One thing I’d be curious about is how you plan to use the dining table. Would you want seating on the other sides as well? If so, that immediately creates another obstruction — not only in relation to the main entry into the room, but also along the working route between the sink and the hob. Those circulation routes are really important in kitchens, particularly in older apartments where room proportions can already be challenging. This is often where layouts start working against you rather than with you. On paper they can look efficient, but in real life they feel tight and clunky. In my experience, when that gut feeling is there, it’s usually worth stepping back and re-optimising the plan around how you actually move, cook, and live in the space, rather than trying to force too many functions into one area. I hope that helps.

Of the 19 roses on the top page, I'd only personally recommend four. Sunrise Sunset is an unstoppable Easy Elegance rose that is my biggest climber. It takes a while to settle in and rebloom but when it does it's spectacular. Super Hero is also one of my go-to roses in Easy Elegance and it handles cold, disease, and shade with grace and frequent bloom. On the other hand, Screaming Neon Red is a disappointment, not really screaming at all and not all that winter hardy for me. I've replaced it because I found a cheap end of season sale, but it's in the bottom 10% of the usually wonderful Ping Lim roses. You and I share enthusiasm for the "True" series and True Passion is an excellent rose with vivid color, health, and way bigger than advertised. Mine is 5' and getting bigger so I'll neeed to move it this spring. Ice Cap is my unstoppable white that I plug in several places and it never ever stops blooming. I have to get in and deadhead periodically when the blooms get a little ratty because they're so floriforous and long lasting, but may I have such problems with all my roses! (much better than White Veranda). Easy Does it gets an honorable mention but it can be a little finicky with our winters. Among the others on the top page, there are way better OSO Easy roses than Easy Peasy or Petit Pink. OSO Easy Double red is a fabulous bloomer than knocks out any Knock Out I've seen. Brick House Red is fabulous and a solid mound of color but you've mentioned Brick House Pink is a disappointment. Among the "all winning roses" these stand out to me as winners: Arctic Blue - actually stays that blue/lavender color even in heat, good bloomer, healthy Canyon Road - I have mine near Brick House Red and both are constant bloomers in a small mound - Canyon Road can tend toward Scarlet a little, Brick house is true dark red Cherry Frost is a MONSTER climber that should be coming into its own this year. It's tip hardy even in a brutal winter and has small cherry blooms that should be nice. VERY healthy Easy on the Eyes (as well as In your Eyes and other "Eyes" hulthemias) is a great mounding rose with pink/mauve eye booms that reallly catch the eye (pardon the pun). Mine is healthy. Easy Spirit is a totally reliable white that is among the earliest blooming HT for me. Not yet a great rebloomer but my rose society loves this one, as well as Sweet Spirit (dark pink). Campfire is a totally carefree Canadian rose that blooms its heart out. It spreads a lot and wants to visit neighbors, but the mutable coral to pink/white/yellow blooms that fade to white fit in with just about any bed. It stays small but could be caged up to spread tall rather than wide. Bright and Shiny is billed to be like Campfire but so far it's a distant second though fine. Julie Andrews is pretty hardy for me and a reliable HT type bloomer that doesn't need a lot of care. Don't know if it would be disease free for you, but it does well for me. Watercolors Home Run is a similar effect in a small plant and it's hardy in my zone 4 pocket of the yard. Kashmir is a reliably hardy Easy Elegance rose that stays 3-4 feet and true red. Music Box is a nice EE rose too, though it fades to white too soon for my preference. It gets 4-5' tall. Maurice Utrillo gets a call-out as an easily accessible Delbard Painter rose that has nice stripes. I prefer Edgar Degas and Camille Pissarro and Marc Chagall, but they're all lovely. Miracle on the Hudson has HUGE single blooms that catch the eye, starting at a very dark red and fading crimson. I'm hoping it gets bigger and better flowering with time. Oscar Peterson is another reliable white spot of color, but it must have some kind of fragrance because the Japanese Beetles absolutely LOVE it wherever I have it. I don't mind because it's tough enough to take the damage and I use it as a trap crop in July, but beware. It blooms a ton so it attracts a ton. Reminiscent Coral is a wonderful rose for me and is mostly cane hardy and healthy. I love the relatively non-fading blooms and I'm looking forward to Reminiscent Ginger coming this spring too (I have Pink and Cream too but they're less floriforous) Sunset Horizon is a tall healthy mutable red/yellow/orange blend that is carefree and takes care of itself. Semi-double but it makes a statement toward the back of the bed. The Champion Red is another reliable red like Kashmir or Brick House Red in a similar color with similar health and bloom power. At a pinch, I'd pick Brick House. I love all the True Bloom roses I have and Sincerity is another favorite in truly impressive colors and around 5' tall. True Love stays the billed 3' high in red, but True Integrity is smaller than I'd thought and hasn't bloomed much. I'm totally watching out for Confidence, Crush, Friendship, and Grace this season. True Joy is a nice tall narrow yellow for me. Among the others I have about half of them and they're mostly "meh". Lots of knockouts and the less interesting Drift roses (Coral Drift beats out Blushing Drift by a mile). I've wanted to like the Pretty Polly series but the blooms are so tiny they're not notable. Easy to Please is a dog that I will never replace - I had a couple for 3-4 years and they never bloomed and were ratty when they did. I agree with you about the Ringo double pink - the regular Ringo is by far the best. The Flower Carpets are boring, as is the Forever and Ever Pink. Highwire Flyer is an Ok climber but Fruity Petals is better in that semidouble healthy hardy climber. Limoncello is a joke with barely noticeable flowers, and the Look-alikes are a total marketing scam as are the "Bee" roses J&P  puts out. Bubble Double and Candy Cane Cocktail and Peppermint Pop and PInkerbelle would be fine if they ever bloomed, and White Lies isn't yet stunning or a good rebloomer but it's just starting its second year. Survived the winter OK. I can't get Patriot Dream, or Tequila Gold ,or Tequila Supreme to survive my winters yet I really like my Brindabella Crimson Knight and will be getting several more in this series including Purple Prince. Just my two cents about these roses. Some of them are keepers but there are some real disappointments too. Cynthia

I hate to be a Negative Nancy, but I  think you've got the tail wagging the dog here. Think about what you need in a home to be secure and content. For example: You want your home to be built to last. You want wiring and plumbing up to code. You want it to be mold-free. You want it to be free of dry rot, termites,  asbestos, and radon. You want the roof to be secure and under warranty. You want the windows to fit securely in their openings. Other considerations: Maybe you want it to have good parking nearby. Maybe you want a garage. Or maybe you want a home near public transportation. Maybe you care about local schools. Maybe you want a quiet neighborhood. Maybe you love to garden. Maybe you prefer your landscaping to be in a local park. Maybe you want two stories. Maybe you can't use stairs and want a single-story home. Do you want a finished basement? What is the air circulation like? Do low ceilings make you feel cozy, or claustrophobic? What kind of storage space do you need? Do you like an open-plan kitchen, or a kitchen that lets you hide the mess and/or keep the kids-dogs-cats out when you're cooking? The best home is one that suits the way you want to live. Decoration is the icing; not the cake.

We have a very similar situation.  Our soapstone overhang curves from 14" on the sides to 18" in the center.  You better believe I drove our contractor, architect, cabinet guy and my husband crazy and gave them all brain damage trying to figure out how to support the stone.  Thank you, Mr. Corlett, who has been on these boards a long time and who has put the fear of God in me regarding various design and support issues and always gives valuable advice. Our island is 93" long with a supporting cabinet at each side leaving 64" of unsupported soapstone in the middle.  We used a 2" x 2" x 1/4" (may have been 3/8", DH can't remember) box beam, primed and painted black to blend in with the stone.  Our beam runs parallel to the back cabinets.  It was placed 9" from the back of the cabinet leaving at most 7" of unsupported overhang in the front middle.  This has been in place for 10 years and performs beautifully. Each end of the box beam rests on 1  1/2" of vertical plywood.   The beam was engineered to have no deflection with a 300 lb point load in the center, just in case someone decides to stand on it. Overall your plan looks good.  The only issue you have is that unsupported corner on the right.   Your pony wall or what ever that is called falls short of your overhang resulting in a possible weak spot, or a broken corner in your counter top (that unsupported corner).  If you could extend that wall to the edge of your counter and beef it up or add a cleat, you might be able to use a box beam the same way we did. I want to add, your stone is beautiful.  And kudos to you for picking soapstone.  I hope you enjoy it for many years.  Good luck on the project! ETA: just to clarify, we used a steel box beam, not wood.

Do you mean a floorplan for a new build? Or house- hunting for  an existing unicorn house? I do sympathize because so many floorplans and existing houses have , well, crappy floorplans. Either way, I’d get out the lined notepad and start listing all types of categories of “ stuff” along with brainstorming where you think you’d like to access it, what would be the ideal “ flow”. But also, think outside the box and think, ranking options of different types of builds or layouts  could work ( nothing is perfect). How many people, bedrooms, baths?For example, if 3 baths, then the “ Costco issue “ of TP is nearly absorbed by dividing amongst those. But, if you want to store say, 3 giant packs of TP, 3 of paper towels, 5 bags of dog food— that’s different. Not wrong, but needs big space.If building new abc have a large lot, especially if flat, , that is where you might have the main house  plus a 3-car garage or storage building that are less expensive to build. ( I think). Or do you find a home with an extra bedroom, or basement, and store bulk items there. That  still does not address the entry / exits. I’d distinguish between edible pantry items vs paper goods etc and further between everyday foods and some other staples. It is not easy to have a conveniently located & sized pantry for everyday meal prep plus store tons of other things.  I have a 2 car garage and park 2 cars in it plus can keep paper goods, light bulbs, some garden and home care and sports stuff, some travel stuff. You might separate the shoes and totes/ packs as an important “ flow” issue, and involving entering/ leaving the house in a daily basis , as opposed to going to get supplies to re-stock pantry or baths. There are lots of threads on mud rooms, shoe and coat storage. Still, some of it breaks down to, what choices do people make about what can or should be kept at entry points vs in bedrooms. Like, a family of 4 or six with each person trying to keep multiple types of shoes, special sports shoes, 3 types of coats, etc all by a doorway. Or, where will you enter the home— from a garage or carport, or from a front door? If you are building, then an architect from the get- go, rather than searching for a floorplan, is what many experts here would recommend. I'm so sorry you are in this position.  Not easy, though you sound realistic.  I have a lot of experience with hospice (7 family members) and am the person my friends and c0-workers call to sort these things out. All too often people wait too long to on to hospice, and they miss out on a lot of support.  If you are trying another therapeutic agent, you will not qualify for hospice.  You cannot be on hospice and receiving cancer treatment at the same time.  BUT you most certainly can qualify for palliative care at anytime during your cancer treatment. (My mom had cancer this year, not a terminal diagnosis.  Stage III.  We used the palliative care team at her hospital all throughout treatment to help us manage her pain and treament side effects.) Regarding the questions you asked: 1. Most hospices prefer you die at home.  In patient hospice at their facility is only if you or your family are having a hard time managing the care at home.  Some hospices don't even have an in-patient location. 2. You can still receive hospital care while you are on hospice AND not be given life prolonging treatment.  Your cancer is your qualifying event.  You could still go into the hospital if you broke your arm or had a UTI that required IV antibiotics.  They wouldn't treat your cancer but can treat those other things.  (Or, you can do as my uncle with Parkinson's did when he got a UTI and decided to not treat it and have it be the thing that hastens your death.)  The point is, with a GOOD hospice, you are in the driver's seat and get to decide what you do or do not want treated both at home and in a hospital. Note, you can also continue to have your own primary care physician while you are on hospice.  Don't let anyone try to tell you otherwise.   We argued this point for my DFIL.  You might get a rash and want your beloved doctor to Rx you a cream instead of the hospice. 3. You hospice coverage through medicare will cover a base amount of check ins per week from a nurse, social worker, and volunteer.  This is not round the clock care for your activities of daily living.  For that you would need to hire a home health aide. Some hospices are partnered with home health companies and can provide you with both.  HOWEVER, you have to be very clear about what is provided to you by hospice for free and what you, your your long term care insurance if you have it is paying for.  Hospice itself is not a home health benefit. Hospice's purpose is to help manage your healthcare so you do not have to make trips to the doctor's, so you have someone to call if you have specific medical questions, to help prescribe, troubleshoot, and manage pain.  They can also get things to assist in your home such as shower chairs, hospital beds.  They have a social worker too that can provide coordination of all of these things.  And, they can provide emotional support. 4. I always look to see if a hospice is non-profit and select that over a for-profit.  I think they are much more wed to their mission.  That is not to say though that all non-profits are good either.  (When we lived in Chicago 15 years ago we used Rainbow hospice for my father-in-law.)  They called on two separate ocassions to tell us he was dead, when in fact he was not! If you don't mind me asking, what hospital system are you a part of?  I used to volunteer for Northwestern Memorial Hospital and thought they were very good.  But, it was a long time ago and organizations change hands so I can't vouch for them now. Ask friends for recommendations for hospices.  You PCP might have some good referrals too.  Too often I think people working at hospitals have fiscal ties to certain hospices so I don't always trust those recommendations, though you can ask. Good luck.  I'm sending you thoughts for ease as you go through this stage of your care.

Rosa palustris is the only U. S.  species native as far south as the Florida peninsula, and is quite common in an area called the Green Swamp, in Sumter County.  Most of those plants flower only once, as expected for the species.  But sometime in the late 1980s, I think, I found one that flowers continually, year-round in that semi-tropical climate.  I propagated it from cuttings, and have grown it ever since.  It is almost never without at least a few flowers.  It is in all other ways a completely typical, wild-type palustris, and was found deep in the swamp, many miles from any "civilization," so I don't think it's a hybrid. It is the clone grown and sold by Rose Petals Nursery.  Since the species is native from Florida up into Canada, it has quite a wide range, so I would question whether this clone would be adequately cold-hardy for more northern climates, but I don't know that anyone has tested that. Rambling thoughts: - You'll find that this board is rather universally against wet rooms; the reality doesn't live up to the hype. - If you're not tub users, that's a lot of space you can use for something else. - You're talking about a lot of shower glass to keep clean.  Do consider that lots of glass means that all your stuff is on display -- your ugly shampoo bottles, wet wash cloths, etc. - Do consider niches or a ledge to store this stuff. - Don't discount the idea of a shower curtain instead of all that glass.  A floor-to-ceiling shower curtain looks nothing like its 72x72 Walmart counterparts, and it is highly functional -- allows a large entry area and lets you reach towels from either side of the shower. - On that subject, we've seen too many showers on this board with hinged doors that "cover up" the towel bars /prevent users from reaching the dry towel. - A curbless shower requires quite a bit of space /engineering, and many plumbers aren't up to the task.  We've seldom on this board read about a curbless shower that met expectations.  Consider instead a minimal curb -- that's only 2". - Consider moving the shower to the toilet in a closet's current location -- the shower doesn't need a window anyway. - Toilets in closets are dark, unwelcoming and can be difficult for aging-in-place. - Consider a Toto Washlet (or similar product).  Assuming reduced mobility in future years -- sorry, I'm being disgusting here -- it'll make wiping easier.  This will require an electrical outlet behind your toilet. - Consider that you will likely need a bit of storage next to the toilet.  My grandparents, then my stepfather did, and that's quite common:  medicines, a mirror and hooks for a colostomy bag, possibly adult diapers (maybe even just for going out -- but they'll require space and space at the toilet will be more convenient for you). Where's your trash can? - Standard things you want to consider for aging-in-place:  Go ahead and place grab bars now /before you need them.  Consider sheet vinyl instead of tile -- it's softer underfoot and more friendly if you should fall; it's also more waterproof than tile, as it has no grout. Difference between a dairy, farm-made, pasteurized, and/or raw milk Camembert Camembert is undoubtedly one of the symbols of French gastronomy. A star attraction on cheese boards, it delights gourmets. True Camembert is a soft cheese made from raw cow's milk. But over the years, new versions have emerged, and today you can find Camembert made from dairy, farm-produced, or pasteurized milk. But are all these Camemberts the same? What are the differences in appearance, aroma, and taste? Raw milk Camembert: the true taste of Camembert Authentic Camembert de Normandie is made with raw milk from 50% Norman cows . This means milk straight from the udder. The milk undergoes no preservation or processing. It is barely heated to a maximum of 40°C. All the natural bacteria are therefore preserved. This richness in bacteria makes it a cheese that is good for gut health and overall well-being. It is rich in calcium, vitamins, minerals, and protein. Raw milk Camembert is rich in natural lactic ferments. It has a distinctive taste and subtle aroma due to the wide variety of microbes present in the milk. Highly prized by purists, this cheese, over 100 years old, is a source of pride for Normandy and the entire region. Well-known and highly regarded, it has held an AOC designation since 1983 and a PDO designation since 1996. In terms of appearance, Camembert de Normandie made with raw milk exhibits variations in quality. Handcrafted, it has a unique appearance. Simply put, you will never find two Camemberts made with raw milk that are exactly alike. Raw milk Camembert can be kept for about 30 days. Camembert made with pasteurized milk: a cheese produced in Normandy Camembert made with pasteurized milk is not a cheese from Normandy , but a cheese produced in Normandy. Therefore, it is not protected by a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO), despite a campaign by industrial producers of this typical cheese. Read also : Difference between Camembert and Camembert de Normandie Unlike Camembert made with raw milk, Camembert made with pasteurized milk can be produced using milk from anywhere (France or abroad). The only requirement is that it must be produced in a facility located in the Normandy region. Pasteurized milk is milk that has undergone a pasteurization process. Specifically, it has been heated to 72°C for 15 seconds. This process allows Camembert made with pasteurized milk to keep longer (over 30 days), as all the bacteria present in the milk have been eliminated. Camembert made with pasteurized milk has a uniform flavor due to its high content of artificial lactic ferments. It therefore lacks the distinctive taste of true Camembert from Normandy. However, it is easier to digest and poses fewer health risks, even though it is lower in calcium, vitamins, and minerals. Nevertheless, it remains prohibited for pregnant women, like all other soft cheeses with a bloomy rind. In terms of appearance, this Camembert has a standardized shape due to its industrial production. All the cheeses look almost identical. Dairy Camembert for longer preservation Camembert cheese is made from milk collected from different producers, but located in the same geographical area. Milk production is automated for better yield. Then, it is pasteurized or heat-treated. Dairy Camembert has a milder flavor, but it keeps well and for longer. If you have a small appetite, this Camembert is perfect for you. This type of Camembert is not sold in supermarkets. You will only find it in local cheese shops and markets. Farmhouse Camembert for a pronounced taste As you might expect, farm cheese is made directly by the farmer on their farm (Decree No. 2007-628 of April 27, 2007) using milk exclusively from their own herd, right after milking. The entire production process takes place on the farm itself, from milk collection to aging. Farmhouse cheese is made using traditional methods, meaning by hand, according to time-honored techniques passed down through generations. The milk used is raw or whole and has undergone no treatment whatsoever (heat treatment, pasteurization, or refrigeration). To obtain a farmhouse Camembert with a pronounced flavor, the time between milking and cheesemaking must be short. In terms of taste, farm-made Camembert varies from season to season, depending on the cows' diet and the climate. However, it has a typical and authentic flavor. For your information, farm cheese carries a label designating it as such, except for cheeses purchased directly from the farm. Also read about Camembert : mager

Assume that the extractor will be vented and not recirculating. For the power of the extractor [maximum output], this is measured in cubic meters per hour and this is the volume of air the extractor can move [subject to ducting restrictions like pipe size and bends]. For efficient extraction you need 10 air exchanges per hour so to work out the power of your extractor required for the space you have, work out the volume of the room [H x W x L] and multiply by 10 to give you the power required, https://www.tlc-direct.co.uk/Technical/DataSheets/Elica1/cooker-hood_calculator_1.htm Also the width of the extractor should be at least the width of the hob, but ideally up to about 1.5 times wider so you have a wider capture area for steam/smoke as it billows out when removing a pan lid. The type of hob, ie gas or induction, in theory also makes a difference to the width of the extractor required. Other tips like turning the extractor on when starting prep work so the room air is already flowing towards the extractor instead of when its already steaming/smoking also helps. Also regularly cleaning the grease filters so the extractor works efficiently.

Hi Jack, congratulations on planning your dream home. Wherever you are in Australia, the best residential blocks are where the rear side of the house faces north or a few degrees (15-20 degrees) north east. The inherent assumption here is that the living room, kitchen, dining, and family space are all built at the rear of the house (that's how floor plans are generally done), so the living areas will get the best sun in the early hours of the day! Imagine walking downstairs to the living room and waking up to a bright, sunny dining space to enjoy your morning coffee:) Another must-have is get a wide frontage of the house, as wide as you possibly can. Unfortunately, with rapid development in the suburbs, especially in new developments, the new blocks have very narrow frontages (I have seen some properties with as narrow a frontage as 12,5m, including the entrance to the garage!). Such long, lean blocks of land definitely lose out on sunlight! So, if you are considering a custom-built property, or even a developer-built one, or buying a completed property, make sure it has a wide front! Another thing is to check NBN availability. While most places now have NBN available, but the older suburbs doesnt offer 'fibre to the premises' This means that despite NBN availability your area, the NBN to your home will be dependent upon dated copper wire and that will signifnatly impact the fibre optic NBN user experience because there wont be a fibre optics available from main source to your house (the premises). All ventilation that involves effluent transport to the outside requires make-up air (MUA), whether incidental, passive, or active (with blower).  The air flow rate that exits from a ventilation path is determined by the blower's fan curve (cfm vs pressure drop across the blower).  Pressure drop across the blower includes house pressure vs. exterior pressure.  So without some deliberate MUA, or open windows, you may be gagging the ventilation.  The fan curve determines how low the flow has to be to work with the pressure drop being caused by the ventilation. In any case, the cloud of smoke from broiling or roasting will overwhelm all but the highest flow rate/capture area/hood reservoir systems. Review of hood and MUA topics here along with embedded reference material will help clarify the ventilation problem and general solutions.

Do not accept your contractor's opinion on matters of taste. Do take your contractor's advice on board when it's a matter of code or another safety aspect, or what a decision may add to your cost, or helping to find a practical way to achieve something that may at first glance seem impossible. What size is the bathroom? What is/will be on the floor? What do/will the fixtures look like? What lighting will you have? What kind of tile do you want on your walls? What kind of soundproofing will the bathroom have? Tile all the way up on all the walls as well as on the floor is likely to create one heck of an echo chamber. Great if you plan to call your friends and family in to sing doo-wop, not so great if when you flush the toilet in the middle of the night it wakes up everyone in the house. Having tile will not keep the walls any cleaner than having paint. Both treatments have to be cleaned regularly. They don't stay clean on their own. Using paint designed for bathrooms and other humid areas is important. Other paints won't hold up as well. What will keep your walls dry on the inside is waterproofing. What will keep them dry on the visible surface is wiping down and dehumidifying the room. An exhaust fan can help with that.

Whether it lives up to expectations usually comes down to five things more than the photo: lighting quality, defog performance, driver reliability, edge finishing, and how serviceable the electrical parts are later. If you are comparing LED mirrors, I would look at: 1. CRI and color temperature, because that affects how flattering and usable the light feels. 2. Whether the mirror gives enough forward light for grooming, not just a halo effect. 3. Defog coverage area, because partial defog can be disappointing in real use. 4. Driver and touch control quality, since that is often the first failure point on cheaper units. 5. Installation details such as hardwire layout, wall switch compatibility and mounting system. From a manufacturing side, a mirror can look great online and still disappoint if the electronics and mounting details are weak. If the spec sheet is vague, I would treat that as a warning sign.

The two windows in the client's bedroom faced the two windows of the house across the street, and they were longish windows (150 yo house). Choosing the right fireplace tile comes down to scale, texture, and how well it complements the surrounding finishes. Larger format tiles tend to create a cleaner, more contemporary look with fewer grout lines, while textured or patterned tiles can add visual interest and make the fireplace a focal point. The finish, matte, honed, or polished, should align with the overall mood of the room, whether cozy or dramatic. Color selection works best when it either subtly contrasts with the walls or ties into existing materials like flooring or cabinetry. Thoughtful grout selection and clean transitions to adjacent surfaces ensure the fireplace feels integrated rather than visually disconnected from the rest of the space.

i've never been called for jury duty and i have always wanted to serve.    i suppose it was because i was married to the prosecuting attorney who later served as the circuit court judge. i worked in law offices my entire adult life, everything from family law to personal injury to criminal law. i live in a tiny rural community.   jury duty can be a hardship on a lot of people, particularly farmers.    i remember one time a local farmer was sent a summons for jury duty which he crumpled up and threw in the trash.    when trial time came around and he didn't show up, the judge sent a county deputy out to bring the guy to court to explain why he ignored the summons.    he hemmed and hawed and finally told the judge he simply didn't have time to devote to courtroom shenanigans.    the judge, in no uncertain terms, told him that a jury summons was a court order, not an invitation to be accepted or declined.    he sentenced him to 3 days in jail, suspended, but got his point across. i once worked in a larger county where a man was charged with vehicular homicide.    this was a very well-known and respected member of the community and finding unbiased jurors was taking forever.     it got to the point where the judge sent deputies out to the streets to round up people to come to court to see about serving.    very unconventional but it worked.

Pricklypearcactus - I could write a book. Which no one but me would probably find interesting. ;) There are thousands of compounds. This is a relatively newly emerging issue, and the science is still evolving. Yes, the science exists to remove them (most of them?) - the question becomes how many, to what level, and to what cost. The compounds are in everything. Literally, everything - clothes, food, drinks, cosmetics, the ground, the air - you name it, we're surrounded by them. Water is an easy target in some ways - people think, well just get them out of the water, that has to help, right? Well. Maybe. Or maybe not. What % of one's exposure actually comes from your tap water....? From a large scale water production standpoint, removing them is complicated. For the system I know, they would have to make changes in 2 places - their water intake (the source water for the system), and then at the water plant where the water is treated before it is released into the system. The changes needed to add filtration for PFAS would cost in the tens of millions of dollars. And that doesn't address the fact that the sludge after it is removed has to be treated as if it is toxic, so that adds to operating costs too. Let's say, ball park figure, your municipal water bill would double if they decided to treat for PFAS. I have a feeling for most of us here, that wouldn't even phase us. However there are a whole lot of other people who struggle to pay their bills as it is, and doubling their water bill would hurt. Now imagine the cost to produce the water has doubled - and we find out that the impact of removing PFAS from tap water is negligible, health wise, because again, our exposure to it is about as pervasive as sunshine and air is right now. I don't think anyone is arguing PFAS are good for you. It's just that the compounds are literally - LITERALLY - everywhere, and my limited recollection is that the impact in terms of removing them just from tap water only, without addressing the eleventy-million other sources is, to quote a smart person upthread - like putting a band aid on a bullet wound. If you have well water, and you test high in this area, and you have the funds to address that - why not, you know? It just gets so much more complicated on a larger scale. And now that I've bored you all to tears, I'll shut up. :-)

Carly, When you shop 'Species' crepe myrtle, look for the mature size of the new tree. Your tree, being 15-20 years old is at its mature height so you can use that height of yours for a match. Just for some examples: Dwarf Varieties: 3-6 feet tall (e.g., 'Pocomoke', 'Pinky'). Medium Varieties: 8-15 feet tall (e.g., 'Miami', 'Sioux'). Large Varieties: 20-30+ feet tall (e.g., 'Natchez', 'Muskogee', 'Twilight'). And just because your tree is however many feet tall, it will continue to grow, albeit more slowly, for a number of years to come. So, you may want to take that into consideration when you buy a new tree. A trees width can become variable, considering how many hours of full sun it gets during the day. Another consideration.

I'd need more quotes. Are these quotes for slabs you've identified or reserved? Slab price can vary a lot based on veining and other characteristics. Stone suppliers in your area include UMI, Granite Depot, Maia Stone, Ace Granite and others. When you visit these places, you can ask for the names of fabricators they frequently have worked with and for how long. This will give you more sources for quotes. I would what to choose the slabs, determine the cut layouts and seaming before any cuts are made. And require inspection before delivery and installation. Walmart can print pictures of each slab from your phone so you can get the layout look from the slabs you want. The layout OK and inspection provisions should be written into your contract with the fabricator. Written in ink additions to a contract initialed by both parties will control. Marked up picture copies can be part of the contract. A fabricators provisions as in the first example are meant to only protect him. Not you. The marble you've listed will scratch, etch and stain easily, unlike quartzite. The double sink is not common. Sink directly opposite the cooktop is not advised because two users will bump into each other. Layout help is available if you want suggestions.

The most important decision is NOT who has the lowest cost.  It is who will do the best job with some pretty premium stone. The MOST important factor in getting a good result, is a good fabricator. Ask what trade industry associations they belong to? MIA, SFA, ISFA, BSI, etc. What about continuing education? What was the title of their last seminar? What industry trade shows do they attend. The only wrong answer is none. Do they have their work anywhere public they can see? (Many have it on display in commercial projects, kitchen and bath showroom, or have a showroom at the shop) What is their process? Minimum is they offer basic advice about suitable wholesalers to shop, advice on specific stones, discuss seam placement preference, overhang supports, and allows you to view and discuss the template placement on the slab.) What fabrication machinery do they use? (CNC, or water jet are acceptable, angle grinder snd cutting in site are not) Can you view the fabrication shop? (should be a OSHA approved WET fabrication shop, with zero dry cutting or polishing, and everyone wearing goggles, respirator, and hearing protection. Just google silicosis and quartz to understand why.) What is your process if my home is damaged? What risks am I responsible for dealing with?  (Liability insurance if they drop it and ruin your wood floor, but your responsibility for touching up paint) What if I have an issue with the install? Who do I call? ( wrong color being delivered, or wrong seam location—DO NOT LET THEM INSTALL IT!) Do you have a follow up procedure for repairing chips? What is the charge for that? (Chips are not warrantied by any manufacturer or fabricator, but many good fabricators will do a fill or file the first year. And charge after that.)

What concerns me is this area where it looks like a space exists between the cornice and the brick.  Don't know if it is just the angle of the pic or if this is an actual issue.  If there is a space, I bet it is not due to the cornice but due to the front brick wall of the home bowing.  It is not uncommon in certain homes in Philly to have the front brick wall start to bow and separate from the house.  The fix is to literally bolt the front wall of your house into the structure joists to keep it from shifting and falling off..     This bowing can be caused by a few different things, but is often due to settling in the foundation, sometimes caused by uneven earth or underground springs.  (Much of S. Philly was built on a swamp.  Other places built in springs, i.e. Spring Garden neighborhood.)  Look around at other homes on your street and other houses in your immediate neighborhood to see if they have star bolts.  (They don't always have the decorative star on the end, sometimes it is just a metal square.) They are often in proximity to one another.  Your newly capped sills and lintels could be to hide shifting that has ocured from a bowing wall.

@DDinSB (Z10b Coastal CA), It might be the same idea as the way tomato seedlings are recommended to be grown. I’ve been doing this for years and I’m very hands-on. The roots are supposed to form a solid root ball and fully fill the container; only after that does it make sense to move the plant into a larger volume. Ideally, to produce a strong bush with a well-developed root system, the plant should be stepped up twice. In practice, I usually do it once, and it works well when done at the right time.

I think small roses/bands need small pots to larger pots to give them a boost. I don't think a small hole in the ground would do as well. I think they would start slower in the ground whatever the size hole. I thought it might be a watering issue with the small plants rotting in a larger pot or hole. In Alaska, starting in pots could be warmer soil than in the ground which was a good thing. Down here, I have cooked plants in small pots and need to put pots on the North side patio to keep them cooler.

You pot smaller plants of all types in smaller pots so their roots infiltrate the soil ball, knitting it together to hold it solid so when you repot into a larger pot, it doesn't fall apart, damaging the root ball. A smaller soil ball warms faster to a warmer temperature than a large one does. That added warmth stimulates faster growth. That's one issue you have to be aware of when growing plants in smaller pots in warmer climates to prevent them from cooking in extreme conditions. Any potted plant will require repotting in time. Building a tighter root ball gradually by stepping the plant up to the next sized pot will produce a root ball more likely to be able to be successfully removed and repotted without damage. You don't plant small plants in large holes because you want the roots to grow out into the undisturbed soil of the bed. When you loosen the soil to create a large hole with its amendments, the roots will tend to limit themselves to that looser, softer soil so they don't venture out as far in search of water and nutrients. Providing a smaller planting hole will require the roots to grow into the undisturbed soil faster so they establish themselves earlier. They will become more wind resistant than they would had the majority of their root system had been limited to a large planting hole and their roots will forage for resources over a wider area of the bed. I found decades ago, rooted cuttings as well as bare roots develop into better garden plants when started in the correct sized pot for the plant size, then upsized to five gallon pots as the plants developed to that size, before planting in the ground. It also allows me to see what the plant is likely to look like as a more mature specimen which helps me determine where I'd probably want it to grow in the bed. Will other methods work? Probably. These have worked successfully for me for the past forty-plus years of rose growing.

@amylou321 - so sorry that your gift was not well received by SO's mother and sister after you were kind enough to participate.   I am sure that the inmates appreciated the food you prepared. I understand your feelings toward people who are incarcerated.   At one time I may have expressed very similar feelings, but life experience has taught me to have a different perspective.    The largest incarcerated population when segmented into social risk factors is illiterate.   70 to 80 percent of the incarcerated population in the US can't read at a 4th grade level.   Between 10 and 46 percent can be diagnosed as having Fetal Alcohol Syndrome, and they estimate approximately 60% of inmates are living with Traumatic Brain Injury, many from childhood abuse, so they have impaired impulse control and difficulty understanding consequences. I look at the little kids in my immediate family and am so grateful that they are so blissfully ignorant of hardship.  They don't know anything about food insecurity or poverty or homelessness or abuse.  They have been read to every day of their lives and love reading.  My 5 year old niece is already reading chapter books, which means she is reading better than many inmates.   The risk that any one of these kids will end up in prison is miniscule. It breaks my heart to think about the children who are most likely to end up in prison and what their life is like.   We all feel such great empathy for the dogs in the ASPCA ads who have been neglected and abused and are sitting in a shelter waiting for a home, but we fail to see our imprisoned population as a product of this same type of neglect and abuse. You shared food and a rare moment of normalcy and joy to someone who has may not have experienced much joy in their lifetime. I thank you for your kindness and generosity.

Fissures can easily turn into cracks during fabrication as they are a weak point in the slab. Your slab looks quite shiny, but you say it is honed? I think that current Taj Mahal quarries are mining slabs that aren't as high quality as those available 10+ years ago, but it makes sense as you are dealing with natural rock formation and there must be differences as you dig deeper into the quarries. Don't go looking for perfection in an imperfect material!

Always-on fans remove treated air from your house and push it outside. This means either your furnace or air conditioner has to work harder to rep;lace the lost air, driving up your heating/cooling costs substantially If you are going to use always-on, you will need to vent through a heat exchanger to recapture some of the heat or cool as it leaves the house. The better choice, however is a timer switch that leaves the fan running for a set period even after you turn off the light. You do not need to vent for more then 20-30 minutes unless the bath is gargantuan. The switches work with any fan, so you don't need to spend the extra money on fans that have built in timers. The switches are a lot cheaper than a heat exchanger, and less costly to install. If they fail, you need only replace the switch, not the whole fan. Figure about $30-70.00 for the switch. We buy ours from Conservation Mart, but there are plenty of other choices. Another option is a switch that senses humidity and leaves the fan on until humidity is reduced to a preset level. These switches are more expensive, but they pay for themselves in a year or two.. We have been using these switches in bath remodels for over 30 years -- starting back when they were very rare and hard to find. They work well. In all that time we have had just one failure and the company replaced it under its lifetime warranty immediately. For more detailed information, read Inadequate Ventilation section of Bathroom Mistakes That Owners Regret.

Did you take photos during the construction of your shower/shower pan? The way you've described how the pan was constructed doesn't make sense to me. There wouldn't be a "shower pan" - and then concrete  + thinset added.  The completed are is the shower pan. If a precast shower pan was used, it wouldn't need to have tile added. There are foam shower pans that are "tile ready"  that could be used - however, concrete would not have been added on top of it.  It would have tile installed with thinset. You need to ask your contractor if you have a traditional mud shower pan or a Kerdi (Schluter - or other brands) foam shower pan OR deck mud with a surface waterproof membrane. A traditional one is a "water in - water out" system.  The water that doesn't go down the drain will go through the grout and make it's way to the PVC waterproof liner.  The PVC liner will be over a sloped mix of sand/cement (the pre-slope) - and it will be sloped towards the drain.  The liner is then covered with another sloped layer of deck mud (which is porous to allow the water to drain through to the liner) - the water will be directed to the drain by the sloped deck mud underneath the pvc liner.  It is very important that the pvc liner is not installed flat on the subfloor - or water won't move towards the drain. A weeping drain will be used - it has weep holes in the drain under the tile where water (that went through the grout/tile) is able to enter to be drained.   The second method is a shower pan that has a surface waterproof membrane - it works in conjunction with a flange drain (not a weeping drain).  This type of shower pan will have only one sloped layer of deck mud + a surface waterproof membrane added over it.  Water does not go down to the deck mud - so, there are no weep holes or pvc liner (all water runs down the drain).   Ask your contractor how the pan was built (don't show him diagrams above - ask him to tell you exactly how it was constructed - otherwise, if he's dishonest, he could just point at one of the diagrams and tell you that's the way it was completed). If you have photos while the construction was happening, please add them.  Does your scope of work in your contract specify how the shower pan will be made?  Also, add a photo of your drain - most of the time you can tell whether it's a flange or weeping drain based upon the drain cover that has been installed.

When planning a living room layout, it’s essential to start with the room’s fixed elements, windows, doors, and structural features. These dictate where furniture can realistically be placed without disrupting circulation or blocking natural light. The goal is to create a layout that feels intuitive rather than forced. Seating should be arranged to promote interaction while maintaining visual balance. Avoid placing all furniture along the perimeter, as this often leaves the room feeling empty in the center. Instead, anchor the layout with a central rug or coffee table to create a defined gathering space. Ultimately, the best living room layouts are those that feel effortless to use. When movement, comfort, and visual balance work together, the room naturally becomes both functional and inviting.

Could be many reasons, just a few to list: water gets trapped between the driveway and the house in a grass area, not enough pitch from the house to the driveway, or gutters discharge into the grass area, and without proper drainage, an excessive amount of water percolates near the foundation and finds its way into the basement. Posting a few pictures of the outside will be more helpful.

The old driveway was doing water management work even if that wasn't the goal. Impervious surface against the house sheds rainfall toward the street. Grass soaks it in. Pull enough of that surface and the same volume that previously ran off is now infiltrating within a few feet of the foundation wall. The French drain is worth pricing out. It intercepts surface water before it gets to the footing, which works when the wall itself is still sound and the problem is water reaching it from above. Less invasive and cheaper than excavation by a fair margin. It won't be enough if the foundation wall has a failed dampproofing layer, cracked parging, or a gap at the footing-wall joint. A French drain controls what happens in the surrounding soil, not what happens at the wall face. When the wall is the problem, exterior waterproofing (excavation to footing depth, membrane, drainage board) is the actual fix. Does the leak show up during rain, or a day or two after? Rain-concurrent leaks tend to be surface infiltration, which makes the French drain route more viable. Delayed leaks, or leaks after snowmelt with no active rain, point to hydrostatic pressure against a wall that's no longer sealed. At seven feet below grade with a wall-entry point, I'd want to see the wall condition before recommending either. A contractor-side breakdown of how this scopes out, interior vs. exterior, and what pushes the decision one way: https://home.renovation.reviews/t/basement-waterproofing-in-ontario-interior-vs-exterior-and-what-a-good-quote-actually-covers-2026/47643

The timing is a pretty strong clue. If the basement only started leaking after the driveway was shortened, changing that surface may have changed where a significant amount of rainwater is going. Personally, I'd diagnose the water path first, then decide between improving exterior drainage and waterproofing the foundation. Otherwise there's a risk of paying for a French drain and discovering that the wall itself was the problem.

After that it gets back into highs of 40s and lows in the 20s which is perfectly reasonable winter weather for roses in cold climates. The wimps have already lost their canes and the vast majority are holding their own and waiting for spring to do any more active growth. It could be the start of a Vitricolous lichen colony on your glass.  These complex fungus like life forms also develop a partnership with bacteria and over decades can etch and pit the glass.  If you've ever seen an old glass bottle laying around for years outside you'll see large colonies on the bottle with a green tint to it, common. Could also be Iron bacteria that will develop a halo identical to a petroleum spill.  It could also be weeping glass disease, (yes it's real) and if you can wash it off, but if it comes back this is what it may be and permanent because it's a defect from the factory. Bird droppings is acidic and could cause what you see.   Little splatters of bird droppings that has nearly washed off can still leave a microscopic layer that can leach alkalis from the glass and cause a halo pattern from light bouncing off it.  Tree sap, or any other splatter with an oily makeup can also be the cause, but what I do know for sure it's not spores, and suggest washing it off within the next decade.

Your last sentence of your response post Moses highlights the main issue of how I define winter survival in a cold zone. I don't doubt that there is cane damage in a typical rose after 17F (particularly prolonged periods below 17) but most of my roses shake it off. As long as the rose can regrow from surviving roots, grafts, or canes, I count it as survival. Having said that, I was pleasantly surprised at the number of roses for which I only had to do a modest amount of tip pruning if at all this past spring. I expect it with the Canadians and most climbers and the Easy Elegance roses, but a lot of hybrid teas had very little to prune off after last winter too. I pruned probably 200 roses before I filled up a garbage can worth of canes. In years past, I would fill up 4 garbage cans for fewer roses. The long story isn't one I'm prepared to go into details about because of respect for the vendor, but I had a source this year that sent out own root roses that were quite small. I respect this vendor and have worked with them for years, but the date I had requested for delivery was much earlier than the roses were ready to be sent. I babied them in pots all summer but there were a handful that just never seemed to put down roots and just barely clung to survival. I finally had to plant them in the ground in September to have a fighting chance to put down enough roots to survive the winter, but they were averaging about 3 inches tall and had no "canes" to speak of. They might survive the winter but I'm not counting on it. I've been communicating with the vendor and am perfectly happy with the response. Yep, not very interesting after all... Even larger plants of rooted cuttings I've gotten from friends (6-8" tall) and planted in the fall haven't had a good track record of surviving the winter. If I'm going to plant something in the fall it usually needs to be at least a solid gallon size potted or transplanted rose in my experience. Now that I'm better able to grow robust canes in spring/summer months I worry much less about winter and the survival rate has reinforced my relaxed attitude. I still winter protect with my oak leaves and filled leaf bags to create an artificial "snow line" in this dry climate and increase the amount of cane left in fussy roses. I probably don't have to, but it gives me a reason to collect leaves in the fall that I'll need anyway as mulch all summer. My bottom line is like yours - there may be cane death but with rose ultimate survival it's of little consequence. Enjoy some indoor activity in front of a roaring fire with a good book on Tuesday Cynthia

The light pink, many petaled bloom, about 4", is super fragrant, but the petals are so gossamer that even a moderately hot day will see them droop badly....more so than any other rose that I have grown.  P!us, the vigor so far is not there.  It is destined to come out ASAP. I'm a family of one now, and have lived alone for the last 27 years. I shy away from ever buying anything bare root or grafted, unless it's on a multiflora root stock.  Dr. Huey just putts along here.  Bcause of my muscular dystrophy I ambulate poorly.  I cannot depend on my health to be steady day to day.....good days and bad days alternate.  If a bare root comes needing urgent potting up or planting in ground and I'm off then, the poor rose might as well be tossed into the trash.  A potted rose arriving when my bad days are coincident still fares well. Almost everything I need for the garden, especially new roses, comes by mail since I have not driven in 14 years...cannot control a vehicle anymore.  Home Depot delivers anything heavy like my favorite mini pine bark and stacks the stuff neatly, too. My rose garden is a real luxury few folks in my condition can experience, of which I am most grateful. Moses.

As with most projects determining a budget and creating a plan that fits within the budget is preferable to just replacing one thing and finding that you have created more issues that now need to be resolved. I have seen homes where small renovations end up swirling into much bigger projects than anticipated or ending up with one lovely room in a home where it just doesn't fit. Before jumping head first into more projects take some time to create a whole home style and color palette.   Figure out your budget, walk through your home and decide what you want to change, can afford to change in the reasonably near future.  (Can't afford today, but should be able to afford next year or in two years vs change will be 10-15 years from now or will never change.) Decide on your style and how it is going to work with those things that cannot be changed or will not be changed.   Next think about your favorite colors  (NOT NEUTRAL - actual colors.) Even if you want an all white house - it has to be the right white and that will be different if you want to use muted deep gold and olive green accent colors or you want to use light and bright coral and seafoam green accent colors. After picking your favorite colors, figure out the neutral color family that works with both the colors you love and the colors that have to stay. You have the following choices: Pink beige Orange beige Yellow beige Green beige Greige - falls between beige and gray with green undertones Green Gray Blue Gray Violet Gray Taupe - falls between beige and gray with violet of pink undertones. My two sisters and I like very different colors and have different styles.  Below is a picture of representations of our colors and styles based on wallpapers we each like: The Taupe and violet gray neutrals that make my colors sing (top row) are very different than the greige colors and green or yellow beige colors that make the second row sing.   Both of those can work with darker tones as well, but the third row needs more pastels and can work with clean yellow beige creams, orange beige creams and light blue grays.  The greige colors that work so beautifully with the second row look muddy/dirty next to the cleaner pastels and the pink and purple undertones that work well with the top row scream pink next to the third row.   Kind of like your blue backsplash makes your cabinets scream orange.   Your cabinets would have liked cream so much better and would have accepted some greens without screaming, but blue made them scream. By planning we can create a whole home color palette that works with the things we love and the things that have to stay without making expensive mistakes. My niece recently bought a new home.   She had a lot of things that needed to be done immediately  (electrical, plumbing, pool needed repaired. . . )  She also wanted the home to reflect her style and work with her furniture, so she had the floors refinished and most of the home painted.   She estimated that the kitchen would get gutted and renovated in about a year - maybe two, so we left the entire kitchen as is and ignored the colors. We picked a neutral paint color and the flooring stain at the same time, selecting a pair that worked with her furnishings and art and decor.   We painted the living room, stairwell, hallways with the neutral and selected a white for the trim that went well with the neutral paint color and the flooring.    She loves blue.  Her husband is color blind and sees blue as a color where most everything else looks gray.   So her art and decor has a lot of blues and some muted greens.   She knew his office would have to be blue and she knew her bedroom would also be blue - specifically BM Wedgewood Gray.  She had that color in her last home and is absolutely in love with the color.   She wanted the master bath to also be painted the same color, but both upstairs bathrooms had been renovated by the last owner and had antique white cabinets, creamy yellow beige tile floors and creamy yellow beige tile in the shower.   Everything screamed yellow when set next to Wedgewood Gray.   The Antique white and creamy yellow beiges also didn't work well next to her hall color (Edgecomb Gray).   We decided to use the mossy green she used downstairs in her dining room (October Mist) in both the upstairs bathrooms letting it act as the buffer between the the preferred colors and the yellow beige/ antique white.  In 5 or 6 years she can update the bathrooms, but we found something that works until she can get to that project. Knowing what she could and couldn't afford to do in the next year and being able to prioritize allowed her to get most of what she wanted and make a few compromises to best achieve her objectives while saving toward the more long term projects.

Here in coastal Virginia the use of grade level "ground gutters" is common.  The problem with them is that rain falls some distance from the eave to a hard surface at grade (typically concrete) and tends to splash back on the foundation.  Over time, the splash back can accelerate the deterioration of masonry foundations and any siding which is in the "splash zone."    You can mitigate the splash back if you install gutters at the eaves and downspouts to direct the flow away from the foundation.   If that's not possible (e.g., at a gable end,) you can reduce the splash back by removing the flat stones and installing a gravel walk way over perforated drain piping which directs storm water away from the foundation. If your lap siding is installed over a vented rain screen that's great, but it doesn't mitigate the splashing issue-- which affects the exposed side of the siding.  Does the less than 6" clearance specified in the Hardie installation instructions affect warranty coverage?  Here's what the Hardie warranty says: "This Limited  Warranty does not cover damage or defects resulting from or in any way attributable to:  (a) The improper storage, shipping, handling or installation of the Product, including...."

The graphic provided by GN Builders above and the language of Hardie's installation instructions mimic the language in the 2021 International Building Code for the installation of wood siding: "Clearance between wood siding and earth on the exterior of a building shall be not less than 6 inches or less than 2 inches vertical from concrete steps, porch slabs, patio slabs and similar horizontal surfaces exposed to weather...." While the area adjacent to the siding may serve as a path, its construction is different from what is depicted in condition "B" in the graphic.  In that condition, concrete is installed abutting the foundation.  There is earth between your foundation and the stone path and there is grass growing in some locations.  My take is that a 6 inch minimum clearance applies.  I suggest you give the folks in technical support at James Hardie a call and get their take.  If you e-mail them a copy of the photos, my guess is that their reply will be the evidence you need to compel your builder to fix it.

U.S. code requires 6" clear below the siding (IRC R404.1.6). If you have impervious hardscape, then 2" clear (IRC R317.1). This is for moisture and pest control. To use WestCoastHopeful's house as an example, the paver patio is considered impervious surface so 2". The rock landscape is just grade so 6". Your stepping stones are 6". It appears the entirety of grade/stepping stones is just too high where the siding transitions down. The vent wells should stick up at least 2" above the grade or you will get washout in them. The primary function of the "Dynaflex" straps is limiting twisting of the tub during agitation., although broken/missing straps can cause an increase in off-balance issues during spin due to the tub being askew regards to impacting the cabinet. You sourced the correct suspension rods?  AquaSmart rods have different dampening characteristics than non-AquaSmart F&P toploaders. AquaSmart (Phase 7 and above toploaders) don't have a physical sensor switch for off-balance detection, it is via "bump detect" code in the motor control software that reacts to RPS signals.  A bad RPS can cause off-balance issues. 1/4" tub movement presumably refers to lateral motion, not vertical (floating upwards during fill and downwards at drain to disengage/re-engage to the spin drive cog). Correct weight of the basket relates to the sealed balance rings having a correct fill of water (it hasn't leaked out). Can you somehow get eyes-on the source of the water leaking?  At what point during operation does it occur?

Layout precedes decor. The current layout is terrible with sofa blocking the window. Decor isn't going fix that. Usually a sofa is placed on the longest unbroken wall or floating in the room. In a small space, every piece needs to have a job.  Or Layout #2: --Float sofa to face the two windows. Put a narrow sofa table behind it to create a landing spot for keys, mail, etc. This gives you an entryway, which you don't currently have. --Place TV to the left of the windows. --Get rid of dead decor items like fake plant, dried stuff in the vase, etc. You have a small space. The corner is always a fight between accessibility and volume of storage.  The 36" Super Susan is the winner for both, for cabinets with equal distance on either side of the corner. It's often adapted in custom to being a tall corner pantry with turntable, as it holds so much.  The turntables can be segmented, with pull out sections, but while that adds organization, segmentation reduces volume of storage. Drywall (paper-faced gypsum board) and a good paint is usually sufficient above a shower surround. Only when you are within the direct water spray does it have to be a material that is not paper-faced. The main issue is it is too humid. The fan needs to be working properly and run long enough. There also may be some errant spray above the surround, as usually you see the "splotches" of mold like you have near the ceiling, not the streaks at the bottom. So apparently water has sat on the transition. You can cut off the paper face and remud if it's just surface mold and the gypsum is intact. Or you can cut out a portion if it's bad. Or you can replace the entire section above the surround with purple or green drywall (moisture resistant). I don't know if tiling just above the surround is worth it for the benefit.

1- Try putting a very long level (3 feet) on the floor in several directions to see how much slope the shower floor currently has. I'd first try to prove whether existing walls are beyond repair. Find an out of the way spot and use a drywall sander on the texture and/or skim coat over an area. Replacing all the drywall is a huge and messy task that involves removing and reinstalling trim. Adding 1/4" drywall is a problem as all of trim will either need to be redone or it'll be recessed which usually looks bad. And all of the electrical boxes have to be extended.

The first thing I noticed was the tight garage. I think the car on the right will need to be a convertible so you can climb out of it without opening the doors. Then you'd  need to climb over the hood of the other vehicle to enter the house. The shared bathroom between BR4 and BR5 would function better as a bath with a single entry from the hall to avoid accidental intrusions or lockouts. The WICs in the first floor BRs and BR4 and 5 don't look like they will actually function as walk-ins, since the dotted lines typically signify where the closet rod is and hanging clothes will come out about another 10-12" from there. Try drawing the dimensions on graph paper and then draw in 2' of hanging space for each rod location, remembering that the corners will be void if you try to have perpendicular rods. Consider where you will store TP, towels, and cleaning supplies for all bathrooms, hopefully somewhere handy to each bath, and where you will place towel hooks or bars. Also think about how you'll vent the dryer (placing it on an outside wall would be better.) All in all, I'd say to consider how this will live for you doing everyday tasks like carrying groceries in from the car. I think you can do better and I agree with those who say to bring a list of wants and needs to an architect.

GLP-1 is a natural hormone your body releases after you eat. It helps control blood sugar and appetite. GLP-1 medications are synthetic versions of this hormone, and they often reduce appetite and food cravings.  However, GLP-1 drugs do not work the same for everyone. People with obsessive or compulsive eating patterns can have mixed results, based on what I witnessed. GLP-1 medications are not treatments for psychological or behavioral eating disorders, or for other mental health conditions that drive eating behaviors. They also do not cure these disorders and are not psychiatric medications.  In cases where eating is strongly influenced by conditions like OCD, anxiety, or other mental health issues, therapy and sometimes psychiatric medications may be needed. This is why it’s important to see a healthcare provider for a full evaluation and not an online service. Of the six people I witnessed using the drug, two did not lose any weight. One has had OCD since childhood, and another has severe social anxiety. In their cases, GLP-1 medication alone did not lead to any weight loss, and trying to get either one to take a walk would be like teaching a rock how to swim.

Second thing is always buy power units, not manual.  While many people think the power ones will have issues down the road, the opposite is true.  The motors in the power units gently lift/lower the footrest whereas manual ones usually get slammed back and forth (which eventually pops the rivets in the mech requiring a full mechanism replacement).  In my store (now retired) I used to order 20 or so replacement mechs for clients each year.   I would order one power mech every ten years! No one makes a recliner unit better than Hancock and Moore, I've carried them all.  They will also be at the higher end, cost-wise.  In fact, I have two new recliners from H&M arriving at my house a week from today - I won't buy anything else for my home. Here's a tip no one tells you about.  Make SURE before you order you have a clear delivery path and openings for doors and passageways at least 33 1/2" wide.  Dual Recliners are very heavy and hard to deliver, they cannot be twisted and turned like non-motion sofas - many are pushing 300 lb.  They are nearly impossible to move up and down interior staircases.  If you have tight spaces or stairs to go up, consider ordering them modular. They cost more when the come in pieces, but are far easier to handle. Good luck!

Any adhesive capable of securing head will dissolve finish negating all the efforts above and allow rust to start over.   I suggest securing head to fence with  masonry anchors.   If you are uncomfortable working with masonry anchors, here's an alternate.  Secure head to a piece of treated wood with screws the use construction adhesive to secure wood to wall.

To narrow them down, a few questions: - How much tolerance you have for maximalism vs minimalism and a mix of colors and surfaces? - How much you want your lines of the cabinets and pattern of the counters to be the feature versus your eye going to the splash instead? - Do you have inspo pics to post here from kitchens you originally liked when you started your project? - Will your bead board splash be color matched to your cabinet paint color? You have a lot going on with bead board, shelving, a bank of small drawers, hood details, farmhouse sink.  That's enough for me.  I'd keep it simple by running a lip of your counter up the wall as a splash say 4"-6" tall, and then just behind the range, run it 12"-14" tall.  (Hopefully you have enough stone for this.) Paint the rest of the splash area the same color as your cabinets. I have done this in three kitchens now.  We are active cooks and my husband splatters grease and sauce on the painted splash.  It wipes up just as easily as with tile.  Paint IS a protective surface.  Tile is not needed. I love the combo of intricate and minimal.  It feels clean yet historic-ish.  But, that might not be your taste. I noticed you saved this pic.  If this is still a look you are drawn to, then a white match to your cabinets is an easy answer.

I'm guessing from the forums you chose to post your question,  you would like something fragrant that attracts butterflies. One possibility is butterfly bush. You would need to choose one that is both sterile and compact. Be careful, as most of them would get too large for that area and the common ones at box stores are probably not sterile cultivars. Otherwise, you will get WAY too many seedlings. If you live in the Pacific Northwest, they are quite invasive. I believe they only sell approved sterile cultivars in Washington and Oregon. I live in Missouri and they don't cause as much of a problem here but sterile is still best. Then - I think it would be happier in a large container with thick sides rather than in the ground because they like good drainage. Removing dead blooms will help it bloom better and prevent seedlings which are still possible even with a sterile variety but it's much easier with a small butterfly bush rather than one that grows over your head.

More on sterile butterfly bushes - Sooner Plant Farm has a good list of cultivars and they're linked so you can see the mature size. Even though you're in zone 7, the general rule is to plant something 2 zones hardier if you're planting in a container. So you would need one that is hardy to zone 5 for it to survive the winter in zone 7 in a container. Even then, you might want to move it to a sheltered spot over winter. https://soonerplantfarm.com/Blog-Post/Not-All-Butterfly-Bushes-Are-the-Same

My wealthy neighbor uses the supposed "best landscaper in the county".  He had this guy do some hardscaping a little over 15 years ago.  After a patio was built about 25' from a junk a-- maple - I think a norway maple - I literally saw with my own eyes, this 'best landscaper' level up almost the entire root zone of the maple with maybe 4-6" of top soil.    So that the area around the patio would be level with it. Even back then I knew this was a bad idea.  I warned my neighbor it was known to be very damaging to a tree to have that done.   He scoffed.  How could I know more than the 'best landscaper' in the most hayseed county along the I-95 BosWash corridor???  ROTFL. Sure enough, within 2 seasons, branches were visibly dying, and by about 5-6 years he had to have the whole thing removed. I will also say that from personal experience, when I've tried to plant something in a slight mound of externally added soil, in the root zone of a strong growing tree, the roots often grow up into that substrate surprisingly fast. In your case - good luck getting even 2" of top soil to stick on such a steep slope.  If I were stuck in this scenario and wanted anything even remotely egotistical like azaleas to grow, I'd sever some of the roots with a ditch witch.  It's a little risky, but with a tough tree like that you can probably remove 1/5th to 1/4 of the roots w/in 5-8' of the trunk.  Of course it will slightly reduce the overall ability of the root system to anchor, and the trade off may not be worth it near a house!  Mine was near my driveway, but not my house.  (I have 3 acres)  I did that 2 seasons ago with a Prunus serotina and it was perfect timing.  It hugely reduced drought stress on some elepidote rhodies I'd had no choice but to plant north of it, 20 years ago, since it was a shade tree I planned to keep, at least for a couple decades.  Never had to water them in the past 2 dry summers, while in maybe 2018 or 2019 we'd had a less serious dry spell when their leaves started curling.   We've had some incredibly intense thunderstorms since then, and the tree hasn't toppled over or I wouldn't be talking about it.  🤣
