Dan, your doing right with the compost and organic matter but if your soil is Edward Plateau your problem is definitely going to be water retention.  If you live in one of the towns in a valley of a river then It could also be a thick layer of silt (minerals) from thousands of years of river flooding on top.  In either case the clay type in Edward Plateau soil has a lower water holding capacity, and any silt will only hold  about 30% of it's weight in water while Organic matter can hold 3 to 5 times it's weight in water.  So you're right to say , when your OM breaks down the soil is losing water retention capacity. I lived in Bosque County and owned 20 acres. so kind of know what soil you have, and also had land in a river valley a few miles away, different at the tops but the same below.   It can be fixed if your garden area isn't very large and you are willing to do the work along with spending money to  fix it.  But whatever you have at the top, Below the top is going to be crumbled limestone fragments with no holding capacity at all, so late in the season it's like watering a rock pile. for growing Vegetables and retaining water you really need at least 6" of good top soil and preferably 12".  Mixing the right clay, in the right amount, will give you water retention that is a permanent solution.  Before anyone starts beating a drum how Clay makes concrete I say you don't know what you don't know.  There are many types of clay that react differently to swelling and some are suited for soil amendments better than others based on your needs. Montmorillonite clay is considered the gold standard for moisture retention and is a weathered type of volcanic ash found in several states but a little on the expensive side.  Bentonite clay (which is primarily montmorillonite) is a cheaper alternative sold everywhere but has higher swelling properties and is commonly used in AG soil.   Over application of bentonite can cause poor drainage and and compaction problems so the amount incorporated and mixing instructions are important.  Learn your clay types and how to use them to fix the problem.  Adding organic matter is still important even with the clay should be added yearly, the Clay is once and done. If I still lived on my Texas land and know what I know now, and wanted a small garden plot this is what I'd do.   I'd Buy or make Biochar and mix in 10% by volume or about 3 cubic feet per 100 sq. ft in the top 6" of soil.  You've mistaken humic acid with Biochar___ humic acid will only last a year and not much better than compost while Biochar is what will last centuries and stable.  biochar is easy to make but will need charged by mixing it with 4 parts of quality compost in a pile and water for a month before mixing into your soil.  If not it will suck water and nutrients like a sponge and plants will die fast, then you'll get mad and give up. I'd also add a pound or two of bentonite clay to every 10 square feet, Then see how it goes and add more next year if it's not enough.  The biochar and clay together will drastically increase water retention, which will also lower soil temperature through  evaporative cooling.  I'd also lower the PH to at least 7.  Your PH is to high, 8 isn't 1x higher than 7 but is 10x higher than 7, and this is how the PH scale works. Your soil is rich in calcium carbonate which is a strong buffer against acidification.  To lower it from 8 to 7 you would need to mix about 1-1/2 pounds of elemental sulfur per 100 sq. ft. 6 to 8" deep to get the PH down, BUT this is to much for one application!  It needs to be split between multiple applications 3 to 6 months apart to avoid soil and plant damage, and it will need to be repeated ever couple of years based on PH tests. The biochar and clay are stable but the garden spot should be level and out of a water shed to keep it in place.  The sulfur will turn to sulfate and eventually leach out, so it will be something you'll always need to test and add, along with organic matter.  (Using Ammonium sulfate will help acidity the soil but already a sulfate so will leach quicker). To raise the Organic matter 2% if would take 1/2 pound of dry leaves per square foot and 1 to 2 pounds of nitrogen per 100 square feet to prevent nitrogen tie up just to let you.  Fine wood chips would also use the same amounts because the C:N ratio is about the same.  The maximum amount of organic matter shouldn't exceed 10%. The cost to admen Edward Plateau soil on a commercial scale is just two much work and money and why I never saw any row crops in the ground for all the years I lived there.  You could maybe find some cotton growing in deeper valleys of the northwest, but most of the area is only good for grazing or growing some types of grass to bale.  Land in Illinois can support 2 cows per acre, but on the poor and arid land of the Texas Edward Plateau area it may take 20 acres to support one cow.  You could also truck in 20 yards of good top soil and make raised beds 6" high on 1000 square feet.  $$$. To summarize, add biochar, clay, organic matter and sulfur (correctly) to your soil to retain water, lower PH and lower soil temperature through Evaporative cooling....or make raised beds. Yes, you absolutely can paint them, and it can look really lovely when it’s done properly, especially against a black metal frame. The key thing is making sure it’s done in a way that’s both durable and safe, because stair treads take a lot of wear. First, you’ll want to give the wood a really good prep. Light sanding is essential to remove any existing finish and help the paint properly bond. If they’re quite glossy now, don’t skip this bit or the paint won’t last. For paint, go for a proper floor or stair paint rather than standard wood paint. Something like a hardwearing polyurethane-based floor paint or a specialist stair paint will hold up much better to foot traffic. Satin or matt finishes tend to be nicer underfoot and less slippery than high gloss. Speaking of slipping, that’s the one thing you really need to think about on a spiral staircase. I’d strongly recommend adding an anti-slip element. You can either use a paint with anti-slip additive mixed in, or apply a clear anti-slip top coat over the paint. Some people also go for subtle stair strips, but that depends on the look you’re after. If you’re after longevity, a good system would be primer, two coats of quality floor paint, then a tough clear sealant on top. Done right, it’ll completely refresh the space and still be practical for everyday use. - Georgia from Flooring365

I was already familiar with the general picture, but recent searches helped fill in some of the details. Parts of the San Francisco Bay Area are fortunate to have access to an exceptional water resource: the Hetch Hetchy system, built by the City of San Francisco about a century ago. This water is captured in a dammed granite valley near Yosemite. Because the Sierra snowmelt never enters the ground and has limited contact with soil and permeable rock, it naturally has very low hardness and contains far fewer minerals and sediments. While I’m not an expert, I understand that all of San Francisco and many communities on the San Francisco Peninsula benefit from this water. The Hetch Hetchy pipelines run from the mountains to San Francisco and come into the area on the East Bay side, near Fremont, where they supply roughly one-third of the city’s water. Hayward, just to the north, reportedly receives nearly all of its water from the Hetch Hetchy system. In contrast, the South Bay (Silicon Valley) relies on other water sources. Much of that water is percolated into and stored in the groundwater table, which makes it considerably harder. Even so, many residents live without water softeners, for various reasons, including those mentioned above. Personally, I wouldn’t describe Hetch Hetchy water as “soft”; I think of it as simply “not hard.” It is clear, clean, and delicious—a special treat for those fortunate enough to live in areas served by this remarkable source.

Know your state law as it pertains to the practice of architecture.  According to California State Law anyone claiming to be an ”architectural” Designer or "Design Professional" must be licensed to practice architecture in the state.  There are also state laws that regulate the "sealing" of drawings that were not prepared by the licensed individual. In Michigan: (1) A plan, plat, drawing, map, and the title sheet of specifications, an addendum, bulletin, or report or, if a bound copy is submitted, the index sheets of a plan, specification, or report, if prepared by a licensee and required to be submitted to a governmental agency for approval or record, shall carry the embossed, printed, or electronic seal of the person in responsible charge. (2) If the overlapping of the professions of architecture and engineering is involved in a project, a licensed architect or licensed professional engineer who seals the plans, drawings, specifications, and reports may perform services in the field of the other practice if the services are incidental to the architectural or engineering project as a whole. (3) A licensee shall not seal a plan, drawing, map, plat, report, specification, or other document that is not prepared by the licensee or under the supervision of the licensee as the person in responsible charge.

Agreed that trying it is the only way you'll know, but the problem is likely the evaporator if you have a newfangled freezer.  It dries things out (I know--duh).  If you're quick freezing the bread first, I don't see that you'll have a big difference between the container and a quality freezer rated zip bag, but maybe the vacuum really will help.  I freeze some slices at a time, but usually at least four, in the wrapper if bought, to best identify it, and a zip bag, and other than a bit of drying out, which is normal for frozen cut bread, it comes out just fine.  Another culprit, however, may be humidity.  If humid air goes into the bag or container with the bread, it could affect it.  Also, if the bread is very moist.  The big issue is likely in the freezing process.  That's when the most loose water crystalizes and becomes icy, though following that, there's water migration, which happens continuously, though slowly, with any frozen bread, even in a total manual defrost freezer.  The moisture gets pulled out of the bread and forms more ice.  Hence loss of quality on to downright freezer burn.  IME, whole loaves, even sliced, freeze best.  You can pull off a couple slices of frozen bread and put the rest back.

If I understand the question correctly: Ikea is asking if the homeowner requires Ikea to provide a certificate of insurance (COI) for whoever is delivering/installing whatever the homeowner purchased. If employees of Ikea are doing the delivery/installation, then Ikea should provide the COI. If a subcontractor is doing the delivery/installation, then they should provide a COI as well. . The  COI is actually provided by the vendor's/service company's insurance company. See Kendrah's reply above. The HOA board should be able to provide the homeowner with a COI template, stating the HOA's requirements. The homeowner should send the template to Ikea, and Ikea should provide the homeowner and any additional parties (such as the HOA Board, or the HOA management company) with the proof the COI template spells out. If the HOA does not have COI requirements, then it's up to the homeowner. But if the homeowner is a professional contractor, I'm surprised they are not aware of this as part of their standard operating procedure. Some of the details may be governed by state law, but those are the basics. My previous condo was so badly managed that unit owners were never required to obtain a COI from vendors, contractors, et al. This left all the unit owners in the condominium exposed in the case of damages. My current condo requires not only a COI, but (as of a recent change of management) a completed indemnification form. (In the case of alterations/demolition/construction, quite a lot more is required, but that doesn't seem to apply in this case.) https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/certificate_of_insurance.asp

In my experience, thick curtains (ie normal curtain material, plus lining) covering a window are effective at cutting down on wind from a window that is not that airtight. A low fan on winter mode should help if the problem is heat in the cathedral ceiling.  You may have to find an on-line manual to figure out how to switch the fan to winter mode. I'd look at: 1) Insulation in the attic over the room.  Also look for air leaks, these can suck hot air up to the attic.  Is the insulation adequate? 2) Look at whether the room has fewer/less heating elements/radiators than other rooms.  If you have forced hot air, is the air hot? Or do you need to insulate the ducts? Can you add a radiator? 3) Is the window tight? Or is the cold clearly coming from the window? How much do the blinds and curtains help with that?

It's difficult to heat or cool multiple rooms in a home with a common system and without zoning.  Rooms--even of the same size-- can have different heating/cooling loads due to their exposure, levels of insulation, window area, and whether or not they are over a conditioned space or an unconditioned space like a garage.  Ditto for trying to heat/cool multiple levels in a home utilizing a common system without zoning.  You can install remote sensors and control based on an average of their inputs, but that results in some rooms being hotter or cooler than desired in order to improve the comfort level in the others.  That may work fine in an empty-nester home, but not so well in one where all of the bedrooms are occupied. It's clear from your description that you have air flow distribution issues.  You may also have areas with inadequate insulation or air sealing.  You can implement improvements by trial and error or you can have someone do the required "homework."  Insulation and air sealing issues are easy to identify with an infrared camera.  You can purchase an IR module that works with an i-phone for a couple of hundred dollars.  I'd have someone do a room-by-room heating and cooling load calculation following the ACCA manual J methodology.   Then check the furnace and air conditioner capacities versus the required heating and cooling capacities.  Then run a duct work design following manual D.  Once you've got the required heating and cooling air flows on a room-by-room basis, you can check them against what you have and develop a plan to correct any deficiencies.

I worked in the humane industry and worked with a lot of veterinarians.   A couple of the vets that practiced holistic medicine and one of the vets that, in my opinion, was truly exceptional, all had the same theory on why we were seeing more and more food allergies in dogs.   Years ago we fed all kinds of foods and scraps and stuff to our dogs.   Then we began feeding dry dog food, the same exact food day in day out.   At that time, most dogs would become allergic to chicken, so manufacturers started producing lamb based diets.   Then people started feeding lamb from puppyhood through adulthood and we started seeing more lamb allergies. They all switched protein sources regularly.   Get a bag of chicken, then a bag of beef, then a bag of lamb, then something else.    Some dogs need to switch from one to the other slowly, but dogs who are used to getting different foods all the time seem to do just fine. I had a dog who became allergic to chicken, and then to lamb and then to beef - it seemed anything I fed him for more than a few months after the chicken allergy manifested itself became another protein that the dog couldn't eat.   I started switching between salmon, venison and rabbit each week and the dog never had another issue. I never again fed the same food consistently.   I buy different brand and different protein sources, some with grains, some without . . .  I feed 1/2 a can of dog food each day and buy about 10 different varieties, so they get something different every day.    Their systems are used to the variety, they don't get digestive issues from changing all the time and not one has had a food allergy since I started doing this.  (about 20 years now). And yes - most dog food is being made with scraps and waste that would typically be considered waste product.     Even those bags that claim that the ingredients are human grade aren't being perfectly transparent.  Human grade means the butchered animal was USDA inspected and that the plant is USDA inspected, and that the handling and transportation is done in compliance with the production of foods meant to be eaten by humans, not that the meal was made from parts that humans would eat.  Non human grade  meat products can come from dead, dying or diseased animals.

"Superior" depends upon many criteria and your taste. I sought Fedtschenkoana decades ago for several reasons. Ralph Moore had told me to "not stir the pot", bring something new to the table in breeding. At that time, it appeared Fedtschenkoana hadn't been used to create new roses. I figured it may be easier to work with as it is tetraploid, as most modern roses are. It "repeats", though it's not really "repeat" but a very long bloom season. I love the "ghostly" foliage and the gorgeous lavender tints to the new growth. That new growth and the "mossy" sepals and peduncles possess the most marvelous "Nobel Fir with hardwood smoke" scent which helps balance out the "Linseed Oil" scent of the flowers. I raised a number of seedlings from it with modern roses. Many of the early crosses are documented with photos on Help Me Find-Roses. Ironically, DNA work was done and it has been determined that Fedtschenkoana figured in the creation of Autumn Damask, so it's really already "in there". I do wonder if, perhaps, the "mossing" in Moss roses may have originated from Fedtschenkoana's genes as a number of the seedlings I've raised from it have expressed quite a bit of "mossing". I was fortunate the bees did a bit of pollinating for me some years back. I'd tried raising Stellata mirifica from seed but nothing ever germinated. I'd planted Fedtschenkoana and Stellata mirifica out on the hill in back. They were the only two roses in the area. Mirifica died but had set quite a few hips containing several seeds which were much more developed than the immature ones it traditionally set. Two of them germinated and one survived. It looks precisely as I would expect a hybrid between Stellata mirifica and Fedtschenkoana to look. It's documented on Help Me Find as "Puzzlement", as it really is one. https://www.helpmefind.com/gardening/l.php?l=2.69411 I also find the Yellow Chinese species, Hugonis, Xanthina and Primula very interesting and have been pimping their pollens for some years. So far, only Hugonis has been cooperative. A number of those results are also listed on HMF. My other species fascination concerns Hesperhodos, Stellata and Minutifolia. Stellata may survive in a Zone 6 environment but Minutifolia would not. Plus, Minutifolia is only successful in a more arid environment. It can easily drown from too much winter rain as it evolved where the winter rains tend to be lighter. If you plant Fedtschenkoana, be prepared for it to enthusiastically help itself to every available square inch of soil. Perhaps a colder climate may help inhibit its "colonization" efforts. A heavy soil definitely will, but it will still do its best to colonize everywhere. Forewarned is forearmed.

Ian,  I'm a fan of Fedtschenkoana, as well. But R. roxburghii plena, the Chestnut Rose, is probably my favorite species rose. The fully double form was the first one discovered, and became the "type", but the single (R. r. normalis) is probably the true species. The double has some re-bloom, but it's more like "one here and there" than a full flush, lol. The single form never has but the one flush. My double form has had as many as fifteen, maybe twenty, blooms at a time after the Spring flush, on a mature bush. But that's in a good year. So...given that, yeah, for most people a tree is 'plant and forget', the best solution it going to be to sell them things that will 'take care of themselves', like the oak. The best approach to attic ventilation is passive ventilation, low to high across the entire underside of each plane of roof. Clay tile over cleats, which is then over sheathing with roofing underlayment, is good for the sheathing and tile, but doesn't address the attic. When you need to rethink attic ventilation, my first question is, what is the problem you are experiencing? Condensation or mold - find the culprit (too little ventilation, bath exhaust, insufficient insulation, no air sealing, blocked vents, etc). Just higher temps - attics can easily be around 20F-30F higher than outside temp, and that is perfectly fine. O'Hagin vents were created to solve a problem. Namely, when you can't get enough low or high soffit venting and need an alternate location. The downside is they move more air in spots, not across the entire roof plane. There are many houses where gable vents might be adequately performing, each house is a bit different and applying a broad brush for optimal venting may not be necessary because of other details that do not work for the house.

The non-permanent window films that stick on with water are really easy to apply and work well.  All you do is clean the window well, then cut a piece of film about an inch larger than the window in both directions, then roll it up and start applying it from the top down.  Use a spray bottle to wet the window.  Leaving a half-inch overlap (to cut off when you're done) onto the frame, smooth the top edge across the full width of the window.  Use a squeegee to smooth the film from the centre out to the sides.  Work your way down to the bottom until the film is all smoothed.  Use an exacto knife to cut off the excess around the frame, getting right into the crease so the glass is completely covered. We've had some up in the school where I worked for over a year and a half, and unless the students pick at it, it's still as good as the day it was installed. I think the "theoretical" duct placement concern is overblown. In a normal interior space, with properly sized equipment and long cycle runs, air manages to blend. If ducts are both up high and down low, for one of the HVAC functions (heat vs AC), the placement of some will be sub-optimal as that argument goes. Hot air will rise and cooler air will sink no matter where ducts are and no matter which function is being used. I have a custom built house with just floor vents, and another in a neighborhood development with just vents in the ceiling or high on walls. Heating and AC work just fine in both without producing hot spots or cold spots. Edit to add: In situations like Emily's remodeling project, new duct placement is often the result of deciding the most cost-effective approach that's feasible given the nature of the project. It sounds like a pro is involved and the approach recommended should be assumed to be the result of the pro applying his or her knowledge and experience. Consistent with project needs, expectations and budget constraints.

What a great project - updating a 1980s Colonial has so much potential while preserving its classic character. From a contractor/design-build perspective, a few thoughts: Keeping the Colonial style intact is key. Fiber cement siding with a 5–6” reveal is an excellent choice  it modernizes durability while respecting the home’s proportions. If the existing trim is in good condition, keeping it can absolutely work. For color, staying close to the current tone is safest architecturally, but a warmer tan/greige can soften the façade beautifully without drifting from Colonial tradition. For windows, maintaining double-hung units is the right move stylistically. Grille pattern and trim detailing will matter more than many homeowners realize  they strongly influence authenticity. A solid wood raised-panel front door is a perfect upgrade. Medium wood tones typically pair very well with Colonial exteriors. Suppliers many of our clients like include Simpson Door, Therma-Tru (wood line), and local millwork shops if you want something truly custom. Adding a hip-roof portico is one of the highest-impact improvements you can make. It adds depth, shadow lines, and a welcoming focal point. A black steel roof tying into your existing roof sounds visually strong. Extending dentil trim is a beautiful detail if executed carefully. For landing, stairs, and walkway:Stained wood can look stunning and warm, especially if it relates to your back deck. Just plan for long-term maintenance (sun exposure matters). Mixing wood rails/posts with iron balustrades is often a great compromise  classic yet elevated. Columns typically look most cohesive when matching the trim rather than the railing/stairs. It keeps the vertical architecture visually clean. Regarding shutters:Colonials traditionally benefit most from shutters on the front façade. Adding them selectively (front + visible side) usually feels balanced. Wrapping all sides can sometimes feel excessive unless the architecture strongly supports it. Overall, sounds like a thoughtful renovation. With careful proportions, color balance, and detailing, this could look exceptional. Best of luck with the transformation! It sounds like your battery went into a "deep discharge" after sitting unplugged for so long. The heat and smell mean your charger is struggling to revive a battery that likely has a lot of internal resistance. Here is a practical way to handle it: Isolate the Battery: Unplug the system and move the battery to a well-ventilated area (like a garage). If it’s off-gassing, you don't want those fumes in your basement. External Charging: Don't use the Zoeller unit to jumpstart this. Use a standard 10-amp automotive charger to see if the battery will even accept a charge. Smart chargers like the Aquanot often "error out" or overheat when trying to charge a completely flat battery. Get a Load Test: Once (and if) it reaches a full charge, take it to an auto parts store for a free load test. If a battery sits at 0% for months, the plates usually sulfate. Even if it says "12V" on a meter, it might not have the "juice" to actually run the pump for more than a few minutes. Check the Charger: Once it has cooled down, check the plastic casing for any warping. If it smells like burnt electronics rather than just hot dust or sulfur, the charger's internal transformer might be fried.

We're no longer in FL but live in another humid southern state, so I can empathize with you. In my experience, your main culprit may be the age of your house since you said it's new. I'm guessing it's built on concrete slab, too. It can take a year to 18 months for a new house to fully dry out. Concrete takes a long time to completely cure and the wood used in your home was likely pretty wet. No doubt there was rain during construction which got the framing and any OSB used wet. Even after the house was under roof, it was still subject to weather conditions until the HVAC system was operating.  Make sure that condensate drains and downspouts are directed well away from the foundation so it's not constantly waterlogged. Your house is probably pretty air tight and unless you added mechanical ventilation, such as a makeup air system or ventilating dehumidifier, not much outside air gets inside so your current low humidity outside won't have much impact. The shoulder season issue mentioned by others is something we've dealt with, too. A well insulated house will maintain its temperature and not require as much heating or cooling as an older leaky house, so your A/C won't run enough to remove humidity unless you run it very low. If your A/C is a basic single stage unit it may not run long enough, but will run harder for shorter periods of time. Short cycling systems won't do much for humidity. People worry about hearing their A/C run "all the time" but that's actually better for keeping the humidity inside low. While you investigate the causes, it would be a good idea to buy one or two portable dehumidifiers. They probably won't last more than a year or two, but at least that will give you time to address the root cause(s) your problem.

The issue with modern HVAC is that it's complex enough to make people's eyes glaze over when they really should be paying attention.  So, they pick the cheap and easy basic system, that leaves them without humidity control.  Humidity control is a very important part of HVAC.  It's what makes the temperature feel colder or warmer than the thermometer reads.  It's also what makes wood expand and contract, and you have all kinds of issues with the home, including mold. You need to work with a HVAC specialist for your area to add a dehumidifier for your low delta temperatures. That means when the exterior temperature is close to the desired indoor temperature.  Your HVAC won't operate, and won't modulate the humidity.  Not without add ons. You have to add a dehumidifier to your system for those low delta times, like in the morning in summer, or spring or fall.  You also have to add a humidifier to your system for winter months.  That is the only way to not have many long term issues caused by too much moisture in the home.

Humidity % readings are relative to how much moisture the air can hold at a given temperature.  Warmer air can hold more moisture than colder air.  65% humidity at 74°F is notably more water vapor than 85% at 34°F. Air conditioning cooling the air causes humidity to condense out onto the colder-than-the-incoming-airflow evaporator coil.  Some of the cooling power produces that condensation effect vs. directly reducing the air temperature.  The coil can freeze-over if the temperature of it drops low enough, with the airflow rate also being a factor.  Two-stage and inverter/variable-speed systems assist with humidity removal by throttling down the cooling power as the setpoint is approached so the system runs longer at a lower cooling rate to continue squeezing moisture out of the air while maintaining the setpoint.

food, you probably know that what's called "speed" for an internet connection is really bandwidth. Capacity. Think of a 2 lane road with a 50mph speed limit. If you want to double the throughput, you add two more lanes while keeping the speed at 50Mbps. The signals travel at top speed no matter how wide the roadway is, but how much it can carry at a time is limited by the number of "lanes". Few households need as much capacity as their internet connections may offer. I have 400Mbs through cable companies, that's their base level. With most modern cable services, the signals travel over fiber optic (they don't advertise that) to each neighborhood. From the neighborhood node to the household drop is coax cable. Coax cable for households in areas with newish (not oldish) cable equipment can usually carry bandwidth well in excess of what any household node would use.  On Super Bowl Sunday, maybe max bandwidth is compromised because everyone is watching TV. I download podcasts to my PC (it suits my usage pattern) and the download rate is noted. Even with 400Mbps capacity, it rarely exceeds 75. Ditto for info coming from your average website - they don't serve up at higher rates because they don't have to and some connections can't handle it. Older modems and routers can also compromise throughput rates. It's true that a 100% fiber connection reacts more quickly (lower latency) but the speed of a download is more a function of the source than the connection. Unless one has a very low bandwidth connection or is living in a household with 10 simultaneous gamers or HiRes TV watchers, the actual capability is rarely a factor.

You are describing latency, which is responsiveness. Not the phenomenon most people misconstrue to be "speed".  If you run a speed test on the connection, the latency is described with the label "Ping". A lower number, measured in milliseconds(ms), means more responsiveness, a quicker connection to reply. Not faster download speed.  The latency is affected by many different factors, but in general, a fiber optic connection has less.

Food,  there are many reasons why speeds would change and will depend on how much traffic is on the network, what your priority level is based on your phone plan, and the level of the phones build.  Phones have modems integrated on a chip that also rely on a number of factors, such as cores, clock speed of the processor, and RAM.  Bandwidth matters, and for cable it will vary based on traffic since it's shared with the neighbors and some other reasons while Fiber can bottleneck at the router and narrow the bandwidth.  For wireless signals to your phone bandwidth can shrink because of distance, interference and congestion.  In all cases speed will vary. Cheap phones, along with cheap routers may not process the data packets fast enough so will send a signal back to the server to slow down the data.  A packet contains 1500 bits of information with about 30 bits used for information on how to unpack and what to do with the data.  If it slows down, and your phone isn't a flagship phone, chances are the phone itself is regulating data download speed. In the case of a router for home networking it will do the same thing, but will work it's hardest to keep up and the demand and become hot when overloaded. Any phone plan form a discount carrier will throttle down your download speed by default, so if you want fast data transmission you'd better pick a better carrier with a more expensive plan to get it.  I have an ATT go phone plan, and had it for 25 years.  My download speed is always less than 2 Mbps but I don't need anything faster so I have no need to pay extra to get faster speed.

To expand on PPF's question: What are your specific goals for the remodel? What drives you crazy about the old kitchen? What works now? For example, in our first kitchen remodel, here were the goals: - Increase/improve storage space - improve function (more prep space between sink and range) - exhaust the range hood to the outside - make all base cabinets drawers - reduce clutter from the counters (like toaster, knife blocks, phone chargers) - provide a place for office supplies (pens, stapler, envelopes, file drawers etc), since I was removing a small desk from the space As I worked on the layout, the most important thing I did was generate a detailed storage plan, assigning a place in the new kitchen for virtually everything (perhaps Beuhl will share their fantastic storage plan!) I put thing near their point of use: knives, cutting boards, colanders, trash near the sink; pots and pans, cooking utensils, spices and oils, and potholders near the range. Items used infrequently were put on top shelves; items used every day got "prime real estate". The storage plan did a LOT to help me develop the layout. For example, our kitchen was U-shaped, so I had 2 corners to deal with. One got a super susan for small appliances (that one was easy). The other was between sink and range, and not a lot of space on either side of the corner. I looked at every fancy base corner storage solution I could find, and nothing suited our needs. Most corner storage is for things you don't use every day, or bulky items. I already had space for things like that - what I needed was a place for things I used every day. I ended up voiding the corner, with a drawer stack on each side. That corner space was not "wasted", because the space on each side of the corner was used so much more efficiently. I say all this because your question of all windows vs. upper cabinets comes down to your specific storage needs.

BTW, your aisles are measured incorrectly.  They're measured to/from the cabinet boxes, not the items stick out into the aisles the farthest.  (You see that when you blow it up.) Aisles are measured to/from the items that stick out into the aisle the farthest - counter overhangs, appliance handles, etc.  They are not measured to/from cabinet boxes since cabinet boxes do not include doors/drawer fronts, hardware, or the usual 1.5" counter overhang. Your aisles, therefore, are at least 3" narrower than think they are. Minimum work aisle widths: For an aisle with seating on both sides (e.g., table and island), 60" b/w the table and island counter is generally recommended as a minimum.

Keep the DW out of the primary Prep Zone, prepping over a running DW or having to get out of the way if someone wants to unload or load the DW (even if it's for only a couple of items) can, at best, be annoying and, at worst, uncomfortable (think of hot air venting from the DW). The primary Prep Zone is the 45" of counterspace b/w the sink and range and includes a 2-bin trash pullout (trash + recyclables). The island is not a very good option for a Prep Zone b/c it has no water, so it's a "tertiary" Prep Zone. The second sink is in a Snack & Coffee/Tea Center where it can be used for handwashing, etc., without getting the way of someone prepping/cooking.  It can also function as a secondary Prep Zone b/c it has a sink. The MW and a small under-counter beverage refrigerator is also in the Snack & Coffee/Tea Center.  Alternately, you could put in a refrigerator and freezer drawer there, which ever would work best for you and your family.  Someone getting coffee, tea, or a snack can easily use the Center without, again, getting in the way of someone prepping or cooking. There is a 12"W Utility cabinet for a broom, swifter, cleaning supplies, etc., in the Kitchen for easy access for cleaning up. There is also a row of shallow pantry cabinets along the wall next to the full pantry.  It could hold extra dishes, serving dishes, small appliances, food you use regularly, etc.  It's very flexible storage and at 15" deep it's not too deep that things will get lost or too shallow that it's not very useful. Note that the island has a row of shallow cabinets along the back of the island.  These could be for seldom-used items that you want in the Kitchen but don't want them taking up valuable kitchen or pantry storage space.  They shouldn't be much deeper b/c you will be accessing the storage from under a seating overhang (also why drawers would not work there). Seating at the island is on two sides.  More than 2 or 3 seats all in one row is not particularly friendly - it's like eating at a diner counter where no one wants to look at the other people.  Instead, with seating on two sides, people face each other and can easily converse without having to twist or crane their neck. Do you bake much?  If so, you could use the corner as a Baking Center.  I had a corner like that in my previous Kitchen and it was great when I was baking, especially when making Christmas cookies.  I rolled out dough on one of the corner and had cookie sheets on the other side.  It was so easy to roll out dough and put the cookies on the cookie sheets right next to me but not in the way of my dough! FYI...I have a sink in a 21" sink base in my Prep Zone (on my island) and I'm amazed at how big the basin is!  So, that sink in the Snack & Coffee/Tea Center will be very useful for many different tasks! Note that most cabinet measurements are suggestions, I recommend making a Storage Plan once you finalize a layout to determine what type of storage you want.  I do highly recommend the vast majority of you base cabinets be drawer bases.  But, don't necessarily stick with the standard 3-drawer drawer bases.  You can mix it up with 2 drawers, 4 drawers, or even 5 drawers, depending on what you plan to store in each drawer base.  E.g., I recommend things like foil/plastic bags/wax paper, etc., be stored in a shallow drawer so you don't have to stack them and, therefore, it's easy to grab exactly what you want.    Based on my experiences in my previous and current Kitchens, I'm a big proponent of a separate prep sink, so if are OK with one in the island, I recommend one on the left end, but it's up to you.  If you do that, then maybe reduce the sink in the Snack & Coffee/Tea Center to 18". The Cleanup Sink would be for someone cleaning up The island prep sink would be for someone prepping and cooking The Snack Center sink would be for someone washing their hands or for the Coffee or Tea of for the MW or for others to use when you have company without getting in your way while prepping and/or cooking.

"It might be cost prohibitive to move the sink to that wall" Do you have a basement or crawl space under the Kitchen OR are you on a slab? Again, if you have a basement or crawl space, you should be able to add the water. Something else to think about - if you're spending all the money ($$$$) to extend the house 8' and redo the Kitchen, do it right, don't make do. Before you give up - I think you will find it's a bad lower element. That error is common to both the Thermistor and the element - and of the two, the element is overwhelming more common. Lime precipitates and builds up on the bottom element. At some point the lime gets to be enough that the water can't cool the element and it burns out. When that happens, there is only the hot water in the top several inches that's being heated by the top element and so hot water runs out quickly. Replace the bottom element. You will notice that it's buried in lime sludge when you pull it out and may even be broken. If you have an amp clamp, you can always check to see if the lower element is working to confirm it's bad (or not).

And use light fixtures that hang down on skinny wires the same color as your walls.   Reduce your color changes. Dirty Sock Syndrome is merely a suggestive type smell as this is what the smell most often resembles, however due to how you live, how you operate the AC and Heat what type of system it is... heatpump with electric strip heat, gas furnace with AC or even straight AC with electric heat strips. Florida is a heat pump market so I am going to assume you have a heat pump, with electric heat. That said, any system can exhibit smells doing the activity you are doing switching back and forth frequently from heat to cool and back to heat again. UV lights and or the systems that contain them can cause irritative issues to the lungs if they produce ANY ozone what so ever. So it's important to check that. There are some that claim no ozone production but I'm on the side of not using gimmick gadgets that often do nothing more than part you from your money, not to mention the bulbs lose efficiency and most are required to replace bulbs annually even if the bulbs aren't burned out in that time. Where the smell comes from could be mold growth, but more common and worse of a smell comes from bacteria. Trane was the company who coined the phrase Dirty Sock Syndrome, that being said ANY manufactured HVAC system can suffer from this type of thing... whether you wish to call it dirty sock syndrome or dirty vacuum bag syndrome is entirely up to you. Why does this happen? Bacteria is everywhere and newer HVAC systems have much bigger Evaporator Coils than years past, due to efficiency and changes mandated by law. DOE / EPA take your pick. Condensate drainage... the bigger the Evap Coil, the more condensate it produces the more likely bacteria and or mold growth can occur. The coils are in some cases thicker, so UV lights are probably not going to do much as the bacteria can hide in plain sight even on a coil that doesn't look dirty to the naked eye. Humidity: Another common problem to certain areas as with higher humidity it will only magnify this problem. What you can do? Have the coil professionally cleaned. However, the coil is repeatedly washed free of any cleaning due to normal condensate that forms on the coil when run in AC mode. Have the coil professionally treated? This is a service some have taken where the coil is removed shipped and then treated, shipped back and reinstalled. Probably not cheap and how long this may last is anyone's guess. The manufacturer of the coil may provide a treatment option by now? The cheaper option? You know how and why this is happening because you understand what you are doing that magnifies the problem... and that is switching back from heating and cooling and back to heating and back to cooling. If you go to the doctor and you say hey when I do this (swinging my arm back and forth violently) it hurts. The doctor says: Quit doing that. ( I know this demonstration "choice of words here" sucks but there is no way on earth you misinterpret things. I'm not here to soothe your feelings I think you're old enough to handle it. Hopefully. ) If something is causing you grief limit that activity to a bare minimum. The smell is often gone in time if you maintain the system in a single mode. I have a heat pump at my house (BOSCH Inverter) I occasionally get odd smells from it, smells more like car antifreeze to me because it smells "sweet" is about the best I can describe it usually when turning the heat pump on after a long period of mostly minor AC use. So just realize these smells are just nuisance smells in time they pass when you refrain from the activity that makes them. Essentially the heat is killing the bacteria and that byproduct creates weird smells. In terms of filter use I use 1 inch pleated with 2 returns. The cheapest pleated filter I can find so nothing elaborate as the more restrictive the filter doesn't add up to anything good in my opinion. I also don't have any gimmick gadgets like UV bulbs or air scrubers etc, as I said they loose efficiency and require bulb replacement after about a year of use whether they burn out or not. You decide what you want to spend money on. For me the smell subsides usually within a few hours of operating the system in Heat Mode and then refraining from constantly switching back and forth from heat to cool and back. Which can be difficult living in a warm and often very humid climate. I service the Katy, Texas area.

You will want to pick the flooring, cabinets, countertop and backsplash before paint colors. Cabinets will come in a narrow selection of factory finishes that are much more durable than painted. The flooring will also come in a limited number of colors (buy a few extra boxes for replacement/repairs down the road). Countertops and backsplashes also come in a limited number of colors. If you nail these colors down, making sure they all work well together you can pick any color from them and have the color matched, lightened or darkened to be the perfect paint color for your walls and trim. If  you choose paint color first it will be much harder to find matching or coordinating colors in the items that only come in a limited selection of colors. I also try to guide people to choose colors that work well with the colors they love before choosing the neutral background colors that will go into their home.   You are starting with a blank slate.   Most people love certain colors.   They are often colors that they look good wearing.   (We are vain - we like to look like a 10)   Surround yourself with art and furnishings and pillows and accessories that will make you look beautiful when you are sitting in your living room or reclining on your bed.  Colors that won't clash with your favorite outfits. I often share the example of my sister, my sister-in-law and me.   We have very different coloring.   I have dark hair end eyes, some red tones in my hair and skin - I am a cool winter. I look best in jewel tones and wear a lot of wine reds, purples and teals.   My sister has olive toned skin and mid-toned brown hair.  She looks great in fall colors.   My sister-in-law has a light complexion with yellow undertones (the kind that tans easily instead of my burns immediately light skin tone with pink undertones like mine.)  She has blond hair and blue eyes.   She wears pastels and loves cornflower blue and peach and creams. below are examples of the colors we love and use in our homes.   My main neutrals are taupe (between pink beige and violet gray).   It works with all the purple tones I love. My sister's main neutral is greige (between green beige and green gray).  It works with her fall color palette. My sister in laws main neutral is cream.   It works with the soft pastel peaches and soft greens and both soft and stronger blues. Knowing what you love will help you choose the colors that will make the perfect backdrop for all the art and furnishings and beautiful objects in your home (including you). Color trends come and go, but if you pick out colors that work well with what you love it will be timeless.  You won't have to pick out all new furniture, art and wall colors every few years because it will be beautiful no matter what the current trend is dictating everyone should love. PS. Then paint one cabinet door as a sample (or have the contractor do it) and check it again against the slab.  The degree of shine/gloss affects the way you will perceive the color.  Be sure to look at the samples in natural light.  The light in indoor slab yards is unlikely to be similar to what you have at home.

There’s absolutely nothing “wrong” with flipping it.  It’s really about balance and how the room feels.  Dark perimeter cabinets will visually anchor the space and can feel rich and dramatic.  However, they’ll also make the walls feel heavier, especially if the kitchen doesn’t get a ton of natural light.  A lighter island in the center can be beautiful and feel like a piece of furniture, but it won’t offset darkness the same way a light perimeter does. A few things to consider:• How much natural light does the room get?• Ceiling height• Countertop color (contrast matters a lot here)• Overall vibe — cozy and moody vs. light and airy If it were my project, I’d only go dark on the perimeter if the space has good lighting and enough contrast in countertops/backsplash to keep it from feeling closed in.  One reason the lighter perimeter/darker island combo is popular is because it visually expands the room. Either way can work!  I agree with what Maureen said — be sure to tie in elsewhere/create a connection — that way the contrast feels intentional.  Good luck on your project!

There are no rules about this.  It is all context specific depending on the size and how much light you have in your kitchen, as well as other finishes.  If you post the colors you are contemplating for flooring, counters, and cabinets, as well as a basic plan of your layout, you'll get good feedback on your color placement ideas.

"Standard dining length" is not a measurement. To answer your question, folks will need to know the length, width, and shape of your table, and also how the types of legs you are considering would be attached to the table top. Over time, connections will loosen as materials contract and expand and the table sees use. So whatever is stable now may need adjustment later. Some tables are more stable with six legs than four. Some dining tables sit on a pedestal. The exact size of your table really can make a difference. You have more leg options than T-shape and V-shape, whatever those mean. Do you mean straight vs hairpin? Or tapered? Or angled? Finally, unless the surface you stand the table on is 100% level, you're likely to encounter a wobble or two no matter what kind of legs your table has.

@lat62 yes temp to high ruins the proteins. temp too low it won’t culture and too much starter it won’t set up. I think 1 tbsp per qt of yogurt is about right. I set a pot into a pot to make a big double boiler to heat the milk initially. I hang the candy thermometer on the side and watch carefully. I grew up in a very small community that was almost entirely Quakers. I was the youngest of 4 children, and my parents were in their 40's when I was born....1946.    Both brothers were in the military, and my sister was married and had children of her own. We lived about halfway between Houston and Galveston, Texas, which are about 50 miles apart.  My father worked for American Oil, and my mother was a stay at home mom. She raised a big garden, and had all kinds of poultry and a milk cow.  I had a lot of pets...a horse, dogs, cats, a goat, and a sheep.   I bought 2 more horses when I was a teenager.   I had a little job at the "Malt Shop". I married when I was 19.   My husband was a commercial fisherman, and we moved to a small town, and bought a place that was formerly a dairy farm.  I had horses, and raised water lilies and fish, and always had horses and a few cows.  We lived there 30 years, raised a daughter who was born when we were 34 years old.   When she left for college, we sold that place and bought a place on a bayou....no near neighbors, located between 2 very small towns that many people in the area had never even heard of.  My husband's health was failing, so after 23 years there, we sold that place and moved to East Texas.   We bought a place about 20 miles from Lufkin, which has a population of probably less than 40,000.   My husband passed away 5 years ago.   I don't have any really close neighbors...most people here live on fairly large acreage. I like this area very much.  People are very friendly and kind, but I am planning on selling this place, and buying a smaller place nearby.   I will be 80 this year, but my health is good.   I have had horses since I was a child, and still do.....also dogs and cats and I still raise waterlilies, and fish to a lesser extent.  Overall I have had a good life, and I am content.   I have never lived anywhere but small towns or rural, and never had a desire to live anywhere else.   My daughter, on the other hand, lives in Houston, and likes living in the city.   I am happy for her that she likes where she lives.

OP - I would probably do an air test just to make sure that you don't have a mold issue behind your shower walls.  Much less expensive vs. gutting your bathroom.  If there is an issue - you'll need to address it. I've NEVER seen anything like this before - I wouldn't think that it would be approved to use inside of a shower/tub surround. Then I did a quick search - Apparently, other homeowners/builders have used Hardi Planks also -     There was even a Houzz post that asked about using Hardi Planks in a shower/tub surround several years ago.  A past regular tile pro commented that it could be done - as long as installation instructions were followed + maintenance + proper preparation prior to installation. Do you know how the walls were prepped prior to the Hardi Plank installation? Tiles (some much more than others) also absorb moisture while using the shower and then dry out.  Marblen wall tile has been referred to as "little sponges" by a few pros.  Some people think tile/grout  is "waterproof" - it's not true. This is how Hardi Plank outdoor siding is described: "Its composition actually allows it to absorb some moisture and then dry back out without damage. However, there are caveats: Hardie is water-resistant, not completely waterproof. If water gets behind the siding (for example, if flashing or caulk fails) or if cut edges are left unsealed, moisture can eventually cause issues over years. In freezing climates, panels that stay wet at the bottom (splash zones) can gradually delaminate if not trimmed or protected. In practice, this risk is low if siding is installed with proper house wrap, trim, and caulking." I did see the results of a test that was started back in 2016 comparing Hardi Plank siding vs. a different type of siding (not vinyl).  A piece of each siding was cut and sealed in a thick plastic container - the bottom of each was left continuously in 2-3" of water to see what happened. The non Hardi type of siding basically doubled in size - and wicked all the way up the sample.  The Hardi Plank siding had not changed - the part immersed in water was the same thickness as the top + measured the same thickness as the original product. Now - I am not suggesting that people use this in their showers/tub surrounds - however, it apparently will hold up as long as it was installed + maintained correctly.  The big issue is what has happened BEHIND the Hardi Plank. If the shower/tub surrounds were completely waterproofed (similarly as would be done prior to tile installation) - the interior walls/framing/etc. would be protected the same way as when tile is used.  After all, you can shower inside a properly waterproofed shower stall - BEFORE any tile/grout has been installed - without causing any issues/damage.  No one would leave it that way because it looks unattractive. I guess using Hardi Planks is sort of similar to the current trend to use micro-cement and Venetian plaster in showers (need a waterproof membrane behind the micro-cement). Below is a DIY micro-cement project by Jenna Sue Design:   While micro-cement itself is not waterproof, it is water-resistant. This means that water will bead and roll off the surface rather than soaking in, which is why it works well in spaces like bathrooms. Additionally, micro-cement is a breathable material. If moisture does manage to penetrate the surface, the material allows it to evaporate naturally, preventing long-term damage. This micro-cement breathability is similar to what you might experience with concrete, natural stone, or grout lines in tiles. OR- Venetian Plaster:   After the walls and floors are completely waterproofed, Venetian plaster may be applied straight to the shower walls.  The substrate prep directions are exactly the same as surface waterproof membranes that are used on shower walls prior to the installation of tile. There are also sealers that are used over lime plaster/Venetian plaster (some are waterproof - and some are water resistant and allow the plaster to breathe). Tadelakt showers: an ancient lime plaster finish. Color Atelier has a product called "Tadelakt" (tadelakt is a process used to do walls - but this company has made a special product that makes it easier to use inside showers).  There is a chemical reaction that occurs between the lime and olive oil soap that creates a hydrophobic seal (needs to be reapplied every couple years).

This is from the National Cancer Institute: Everyone is exposed to asbestos at some time during their life. Low levels of asbestos are present in the air, water, and soil. People who become ill from asbestos are usually those who are exposed to it on a regular basis, most often in a job where they work directly with the material or through substantial environmental contact. My FIL got mesothelioma, but he was a mechanic on fighter jets in the air force and they sprayed asbestos (then, the wonder mineral) all over everything to prevent shots from causing fires. Hi, Joe, As owner of a residential design/build company, I appreciate your dilemma, albeit from the other side of the table, so to speak. First, design/build--whether performed on a fixed-contract price or cost-plus basis-- is best done as an "open book" process with full visibility of costs including the builder's overhead and profit.   Ask each company you're considering what their overhead and profit is when building on a fixed-contract price basis.  If they build on a cost-plus basis ask what the "plus" is. After covid-19, we changed from building on a fixed-contract price to a fixed-management fee basis.  Our clients pay for all of the costs associated with building their home plus our fixed fee to management the process.  While they're at risk for increases in material or subcontracted labor versus our estimate, we don't put any more in our pocket when those occur. Estimating construction costs is a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem:  the builder can't produce a reasonably accurate estimate without plans, and the client doesn't want to spend money to produce plans for a home that won't get built.   We do cost benchmarking prior to design.  Our benchmarking process compares plans and actual construction costs for homes we've built in the last year or two which are similar to what the client has in mind.  For each plan, we determine what is different from the client's intended home design and make estimates of the cost of those differences (e.g., three-car vs. two-car garage, larger home footprint, site work costs, etc.)  Then we add an amount for whatever construction cost inflation we've had in our market since the homes were built.  It's not perfect, but it's a fairly quick reality check before investing anything in a design.

“We understand that there are too many fake seeds in the market. We ourselves have got a lot of fake seeds from our Chinese Plant seeds suppliers. Honestly we cannot assure you that all our seeds are 100% authentic, due to similarity and identification confusion on plant itself. But we are ready to take responsibility of all Chinese plant seeds wholesale we offer. For each order, we will send clear pictures of seeds to you before we ship out the seeds. If you don’t agree with authenticity of certain species, we will refund you 100%.” That sounds reasonable. “Came across …” Is this another case of ”they found you”?

So, this is a company located in China. They state this fact on their web site. Quote: "We ship seeds via Express Mail Service of Chinese Post Office." So, ask yourself: how is it possible that bare root roses are being shipped to the USA from China and follow USDA import regulations? There is absolutely no mention of Phytosanitary protocols being observed. In fact, there is precious little information about who they are and how they do what they do. I take that as deliberate obfuscation. Remember, if you receive illegal plant material, you are the importer of record and can be fined or have plants destroyed. Roses imported from China MUST be accompanied by the proper Phytosanitary documentation or it is an illegal transaction. One possible (likely) scenario is that they are simply buying product from American suppliers and having them drop-ship to US customers, all happening within the USA. They say that when buying roses from them, add an additional 35 days for delivery, so.... Who knows what is actually happening here. Also worth noting is that they felt it necessary to include a DMCA Statement page, suggesting that they may have "inadvertently" used intellectual property on their web site that they do not have permission to use. "As for description and pictures of different species on the web, we cited mostly from Wikipedia.com, as well as some other database, which might not be stated one by one. Here we present our sincere gratitude to informative database like Wikipedia." I wonder what "some other database" really means. Basically they are admitting to using copyrighted material from other sites and will observe DMNCA rules and remove things if they get caught. There is absolutely no meaningful motivating reason to buy roses from this company when the varieties they list can be found here in the US from legit suppliers. If prices look too good to be true, then they probably are. My rating: AVOID!

I know this post is a month old but I just saw it. It looks like you live in climate zone 4 according to this map:https://basc.pnnl.gov/images/iecc-climate-zone-map The code minimum floor insulation for an uninsulated floor is R19, but that is the minimum; you could always add more. This website has the minimums:https://www.energy.gov/energysaver/insulation From your description, it sounds like your ducts are outside of the conditioned space and there is no easy way to get them into the conditioned space if you only insulate the floor, whether between the joists or some sort of continuous insulation under the joists. You live in a cold climate and you’ll be running your heated air )that you paid to heat,) outside in the winter, before it comes back inside. You’re going to lose a lot of heat unless you can figure out a way to totally air seal the ducts and get a lot of insulation onto them. If you are concerned about moisture then you should understand that placing HVAC ducts outside in the summer can cause condensation on the cold ductwork. It is highly recommended that all HVAC equipment and ductwork be located within the conditioned space for many reasons. There are many websites on this topic and here is one:https://www.energy.gov/cmei/buildings/articles/ducts-conditioned-space-building-america-top-innovation What are the ducts made of? If they are flex duct, it will be difficult to keep animals out of them because if animals get into your crawl space, they can chew on the ducts. It is highly recommended that crawl spaces be encapsulated and insulated, rather than venting crawlspace/insulating the underside of the floor. Based on the situation with your ductwork, I highly recommend that you pivot and consider an encapsulated crawlspace. An added bonus is that you will more easily be able to access your mechanicals under the house. There are many websites on the topic of crawlspace encapsulation. Here is one:https://www.energyvanguard.com/blog/should-you-encapsulate-your-crawl-space/

"Should I try and dig up what I can and bring them inside?" No. Digging up mature/established plants to bring inside - even temporarily - is far more likely to be damaging or destructive than leaving them in place to withstand the cold. Depending on the plant, remay or harvest cloth maybe all the cold protection you need. Or caging the plant loosely with chicken wire, etc. and stuffing the cage with fallen leaves or straw. Just make sure the soil/plant is full hydrated and use a light, breathable fabric to protect, not heavy or plastic.

Good luck. When I checked into this, I was surprised how low temps might go.  See my thread on overstory protection here:   https://www.houzz.com/discussions/6410966/gardening-concepts-explored-and-discussed-overstory-protection The type of freeze can make a huge difference, but with a nearby storm system forming I suspect this will be the more dangerous type of advective freeze that is harder to protect against. I saw a lot of damaged plants in Jacksonville during that trip.  Though fundamentally agreeing with Gardengal48, I would add a caveat that there's a small group of plants that are 1) very tender with a 2) discrete root system that make more sense to try to take indoors after all.  I'm not an expert on Florida landscaping though, so I can't believe sure what those would be and someone else should provide that level of detail.  I don't remember the varieties but in the Jacksonville botanical garden,  some bromeliads looked fine after their freeze into the mid 20s...some looked damaged.  Bromeliads are generally easy to transplant, as their root system is mainly just for anchoring.  So for example, my south facing garage 'cold greenhouse' is a little too brisk for my pineapple so it stays in a (plant light - lighted) closet inside for winter - it has never minded being dug up for the indignity of yearly repotting! update: These guys are saying coldest in central Florida for 16 years. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bwBvWPOjYYA They mention the winds blowing = advective freeze!

I have been in tubs that are too long and do not find them to be easy to lay in if the toes cannot grip the end or if doing so makes your butt slip and back bend uncomfortably. Additionally, a longer tub takes more water to fill so IMO it is best to find the a size that fits comfortably without being too wide or long. Tub material. Cast iron is supposed to retain heat well but the spots not warmed by water are cold to lay against initially. A quality acrylic does not feel as cold and my experience with builtin is that acrylic retains heat just as well, if not better than free standing cast iron.

I'd vote for a drop-in tub.  First, it's immensely easier not to clean around the base of a free-standing tub.  Second, I like the look of the tub surround extending into the shower as a seat -- it's streamlined and neat, though -- as you'll need a very large piece of stone -- it's an expensive look.  A tile surround would be significantly cheaper.  Centering the tub doesn't matter to me.  I do agree with the people who are suggesting you put in an access panel so a workman could get under the tub for future repairs.  If you plan a panel as a part of your build, it won't look like a bandaid later. Things I'd think about: - Think about your window treatments before you install the tub.  The two tub options demand different styles. - Where will you hang tub towels? - Be sure you hinge your shower door "towards the wall" so you can hang towels on the wall.  It would seem more natural to hinge the door "towards the other tub", but that would place your towels behind the door /inaccessible when you need them. - Consider that your entire shower will "be visible" -- this means it'll be a lot of glass to keep clean, and your shampoo bottles, etc. will be visible at all times.  You can put in a niche -- put in more than just a little 12x12, but think about whether you're okay with that big purple or green bottle interrupting the look of your shower. - Remember that glass showers usually end up with a slightly green tint -- and with so much glass in your project, it'll end up showing.  If you want to use green, you're set; however, if that's not your goal, look into the higher-priced glass with no color tone.  I think it's low-iron glass? - People are talking about aging-in-place.  While that is a common goal on this board, since you say you'll move before retirement, I wouldn't think much on this subject. - I agree with the people who suggest you don't go with too big a tub.  I'm very short, and a long tub (which people often choose for a master bath) is uncomfortable for me.  I'd choose a deep-but-not-long tub.  Consider that a smaller tub fills faster /stays hot longer -- more surface area cools off faster. - I'd never want duplicate sinks.  Even with a good-sized vanity, as you'll have, I'd 100% rather have the extra storage -- maybe even a linen tower on one end.

Hi.  I know nothing about automatic doors, but I work in automation.  If the doors open or close on their own it's likely to be a faulty or dirty sensor that's triggering the door operation.  At the top of the door there will be something that looks like a lens or a rounded red or translucent plastic.  That thing houses an infrared sensor that detects people in front of the door.  If it is dirty, or misaligned, or if some heat or light source sporadically aims at that sensor, it could trigger the sensor and make the logic board think somebody is present. I hope this helps!

All the 2x lumber up there is actually called studs. It is the structure that holds your house up. Most interesting cat_ky , it's not often we see anyone on this forum with this type knowledge so will you please tell us more?   Where are rafters and ceiling joists located in single story homes?   What is the lumber called that drywall is fastened to on walls?

@cat_ky   Um, no. A wall's vertical members are called studs. The horizontal members at the top and bottom of the wall are the top and bottom plate. Short horizontal members between studs are blocks. Horizontal parts that support a floor or ceiling are joists. Parts that run up the slope of a roof are rafters, and the part that supports the ridgeline is the peak. Obviously I'm simplifying things. There are a lot more names to know if you want to have windows, for example. If you google "compound roof framing parts diagram" you'll find pictures and text that explain a lot of this stuff.

Clear all the blown-in insulation when you get the new roof. When choosing new insulation, consider that it is much easier  to find pest problems (such as a dead rat) by lifting up insulation batts than it is by shoveling up blown-in insulation.  Do everything possible to block entry by rats and raccoons.

Hello! You’re already making thoughtful selections, and your goal of modern but timeless is very achievable with what you’ve chosen so far. Backsplash tileSince you don’t want the backsplash to be the focal point, I agree that a glossy tile with a lot of variation may feel too busy next to Carrara Gold quartz. For a timeless look, I’d suggest:•   A matte or satin-finish subway tile•   Sizes like 3×12 or 4×12 are classic and work well both horizontally or vertically•   Soft whites, warm whites, or very light greige tones will pair nicely with BM Natural Cream and champagne bronze hardwareA simple stacked layout (rather than offset) will also feel more modern and clean. Apron-front sink (main sink)If you cook often and want durability beyond stainless steel:•   Fireclay is a great option: very durable, classic, and works beautifully in timeless kitchens•   Choose a single-bowl design with a rear or side drain for better functionalityFireclay pairs especially well with light cabinetry and warm metals like champagne bronze. Island prep sinkFor the prep sink near the fridge:•   Stainless steel is still the most practical choice here•   It visually recedes and won’t compete with the main sinkThis keeps the island clean-looking and functional. Outlet placement tips•   Plan outlets under upper cabinets or along cabinet edges where possible•   For the island, consider pop-up outlets or outlets hidden on the seating sideGood outlet planning makes a big difference in keeping the design looking polished. Overall paletteYour color selections work very well together:•   SW Alabaster + BM Natural Cream create a soft, warm base•   Carrara Gold quartz complements champagne bronze nicely•   SW Anonymous on the island adds depth without feeling trendy You’re on the right track — keeping finishes simple and letting proportions and materials do the work is what makes a kitchen feel timeless. Best of luck with your build!
